speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Acting Minister of Finance):
subtopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not wish to unduly delay
my hon. friend in presenting his motion and reaching a conclusion on it, but I think it fair to point out to the House, and for the information of the Public Accounts committee, before which committee I suppose my hon. friend will bring these matters for investigation, certain considerations. I was a member of the House at the time when the business profits tax and the income tax were introduced. I think that both these taxes are based upon the legislation of the British House, and that it was the desire of the representatives of the people in parliament that in so far as possible we should follow the British practice. My recollection-and I stand in the judgment of hon. members who were then in the House-is that parliament at that time unanimously decided that there should be secrecy, that confidential reports made to the government either by firms or private individuals should be treated as confidential. For the information of the House and of the Public Accounts committee, I especially desire to direct their attention to section 14 of the Business Profits War Tax Act, chapter 11 of the statutes of 1916, and my recollection is that the same clause will be found in the Income Tax Act:
No person employed in the service of His Majesty shall communicate or allow to be communicated to any person not legally entitled thereto any information obtained under the provisions of this act, or allow any such person to inspect or have access to any written statement furnished under the provisions of this act. Any person violating any of the provisions of this section shall be liable on summary conviction to a penalty not exceeding two hundred dollars.
I am not going to oppose the resolution of my hon. friend. This is a new House, and the Public Accounts committee is constituted from members representing all parties in this House, and it will be for the Public Accounts committee, having regard to the

Immigration of Labourers
law as laid down by parliament, to determine how far they should go. I should like to say that so far as this government is concerned, we have endeavoured to carry out the principle of the law and to maintain secrecy so far as possible in connection with these reports. I have had the honour of presiding over the department administering these acts, and although personally I had the right, under the rule that the Minister of Finance is an officer of the department, to look into these matters, I have never attempted to dig into the affairs of firms or individuals making these reports.

PROPOSED INVESTIGATION BY COMMITTEE QN BANKING AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the select standing committee on Banking and Commerce should be instructed, in accordance with that committee's recommendation at the 1923 session of parliament, to continue during the present session of the House, the investigation into the basis, function and control of financial credit and the relation of credit to commerce and industry, with a view to advising this House as to the desirability of some constructive and fundamental changes in the present financial system.
He said: I should like the close attention of the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) for a few minutes at all events.

subtopic: PROPOSED INVESTIGATION BY COMMITTEE QN BANKING AND COMMERCE
speechtext: I am always much interested in the remarks of my hon. friend.

subtopic: PROPOSED INVESTIGATION BY COMMITTEE QN BANKING AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
On the 9th March, 1923, the House ordered as follows:
That in accordance with the recommendations contained in the second report of the select standing committee on Banking and Commerce, the said committee be given power to investigate the basis, the function and the control of financial credit, and the relation of credit to industrial problems.

Financial Credit
In accordance with that order the committee spent very considerable time in hearing a number of witnesses on the question under consideration, among whom were the following: Messrs. Bevington and East from Alberta; Sir Frederick Williams-Taylor from Montreal; Sir John Aird from Toronto; Major Douglas from England; Sir Edmund Walker, Toronto; Professor Adam Shortt, of Ottawa; Professor Swanson, of the University of Saskatchewan; Professor Irving Fisher, of Yale University; Mr. Tom Moore, of the Dominion Trades and Labour Congress; and Mr. H. T. Ross, Secretary of the Canadian Bankers Association Immediately after the evidence of these gentlemen was received the committee proceeded, not to consider that evidence, but to consider the revision of the Bank Act, and that revision took up the remainder of the session. At the last sitting of the committee the following resolution was passed which formed the eighth report of the committee:
Your committee in obedience to the order of the House of March 9, 1923, have had under consideration the question of investigating the basis, the function and the control of financial credit and the relation of credit to the industrial problems; and in connection therewith have held several meetings and examined the following witnesses, namely: Messrs. Bevington, Douglas, Fisher and others, but have not been able to complete their inquiry into the matter covered by the order of reference.
Your committee specially recommend that a further reference be made at the next session of parliament on the matters referred to in the said order of reference.
Your committee beg to submit printed copy of their proceedings on such reference and all documents submitted and not contained in the proceedings.
All which is respectfully submitted.
This report from the committee was made to the House and acquiesced in by the House. It was necessary, however, that the matter should be revived last year if anything further was to be done. Therefore the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine), if my recollection serves me, placed a resolution on the order paper with the intention of reviving the matter, but as hon. members will recollect the disastrous failure of the Home Bank necessitated the Banking and Commerce committee last year devoting its whole attention for the complete session to that particular matter and to various questions arising therefrom. Moreover the resolution which the hon. member for East Calgary placed on the order paper, along with many other resolutions, was not reached, on account of the fact that the government took private members' day very early last session. This matter therefore was not revived last session, and I am asking this year that the committee be given power to complete the investigation
undertaken two years ago. I should like to remind the House and the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) that so far the Banking and Commerce committee has not held any meetings, and, so far as I know, it has very little business before it this year. It seems to me therefore that the time is opportune for the completion of the work begun two years ago. In my judgment there is no need to spend further money in securing further witnesses. We have a vast amount of very useful information already in the report, information which has never been discussed,-which has not had five minutes' discussion in the committee. It seems to me to be only reasonable and fair that this year the committee, with very little to do, should be given instructions by this House to complete the report which they should have made two years ago. Indeed, I am asking nothing further than the committee itself recommended at the conclusion of the session of 1923. If the government were disposed to grant this request I would feel disposed to save the time now by not setting forth further reasons why, in my judgment, the work of this committee should be completed, and if I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to pause to ask the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) whether or not, with the information I have already placed before him and the House, he will not grant the request that I have made. I should not like to exhaust my right to speak, but I would ask him the question now, if he feels disposed to answer it, as to whether or not, in view of the facts I have set forth, it is not a fair and reasonable request that I make.

Mr. Speaker, this seems
a most amusing form for a resolution to take to be submitted to parliament. It expresses the acquiescence of this House in the Banking and Commerce committee continuing an investigation providing it does not make the investigation useful. The House is quite ready in its opinion that the Banking and Commerce committee
-should be instructed, in accordance with that committee's recommendation at the 1923 session of parliament, to continue during the present session ^ of the House, the investigation into the basis, function and control of financial credit and the relation of credit to commerce and industry, with a view to advising this House as to the desirability of some constructive and fundamental changes in the present financial system.
-providing the committee does not get any witnesses outside of officers of the govem-
ment. I know the amendment is put on at the suggestion of the Acting Minister of Finance, but surely the hon. member sees that it is making simply a farce of the whole resolution. The House is to have a continuation of an investigation into a question that is not only vital but so abstruse that the numbers of those who really comprehend it in any country are remarkably limited, and the committee are to be hobble-skirted as soon as they start out. They are told that they already have had enough expert advice on the question, and all they can get from this on is from officers of the department. At the same time, there is an implication in this resolution that this Dominion requires a constructive and fundamental change in its whole financial system. I cannot help remarking on the absurdity of the House intimating that our financial system requires constructive and fundamental changes, and our committing the task of devising those changes to a committee whose powers are abbreviated, whose investigations are limited, into making inquiries from a few officers of the department. Is the thing not absurd?

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Centre Winnipeg) moved:
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, if at any time during the first two years after his arrival in Canada any immigrant is unable to obtain employment. th9 federal government should accept full responsibility for his maintenance.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it will be noted that this resolution does not cover the general question of unemployment, but rather limits itself to responsibility for unemployed immigrants. In reality, it involves little more than a regulation that will check up the effectiveness of the government's immigration
policy. If the government brings in only those immigrants who are needed, there will be no necessity whatever for any added responsibility. If, however, the government's policy is unsound or its administration inefficient, why should the resulting burdens be laid upon the provinces or the municipalities? If the principle of this resolution is adopted, it might lead to a correlation of the activities of, if not to a consolidation of, the Departments of Immigration and Labour. At the present time there appears to be no correlation at all between these two departments. We have on the one hand the reports of the Department of Labour showing that there is to-day altogether too great a supply of labour, and on the other hand there is the utmost activity being put forth by the Department of Immigration to bring in still more labourers. It would seem to be only reasonable that these two departments should work in close cc-operation; indeed, it would seem advisable to consolidate them under one departmental head.
With regard to the question of the acute unemployment that exists at the present time little need be said. This government within the past few months has been literally deluged with deputations from the nearby cities, and with resolutions from the cities that are more remote. I have no thought whatever of attempting to bring before the House the sheaf of resolutions which have been submitted to the government. I think we all recognize that from Halifax to Sydney representations have been made within the last few months to the effect that there is a very great deal of unemployment.
Although I have said that the resolution i3 directed specifically to the question of the unemployed immigrant, it must be remembered that the general question of unemployment cannot be ignored, inasmuch, as if work is found for immigrants in an already overcrowded labour market, others are bound to be displaced in consequence. This has happened again and again through the high-pressure methods which have sometimes been adopted by the Immigration department. New arrivals have been quickly placed, and the department has boasted of their quick placements, at the very time that other workers who have been longer in the country have been wandering about in search of positions.
We all recall that a few months ago there was held in the city of Ottawa an unemployment conference, or perhaps more correctly a national conference with regard to winter unemployment in Canada. This conference, although it was called primarily to deal with winter unemployment, broadened out into a
Unemployed Immigrants

discussion of the whole question of unemployment. There were some fifty delegates present representing the Dominion and provincial governments, the municipalities, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, Canadian building and construction, labour, the Canadian railways, and the employment service of Canada. Evidence was given of much unemployment in all sections of Canada. Mayors and responsible officials from one end of the country to the other testified to the serious character of the unemployment situation in their several cities, and at the conclusion of the conference there was passed the following very significant resolution:
The existing conditions are being aggravated by the present policy of bringing immigrants to this country who are drifting to our industrial centres as casual labourers without possibility of employment. Immediate action being necessary to correct this condition, we urge upon the federal and provincial governments that all such immigration shall be immediately regulated until it is proved that there is a reasonable demand for labour and that it is possible of being absorbed.
That seems to be a very reasonable contention ; but it is a rather strange commentary on our immigration policy that a group of responsible officials should pass this resolution and send it out broadcast, declaring that we have no further need for immigration because of the large volume of unemployment that exists at the present time. It is not my intention to read at any length from this report, although I think that every hon. member should read it carefully. There are, however, one or two very interesting statements made by representatives from the Scandinavian countries. They show very conclusively that these immigrants whom we have always regarded as most desirable are often not easily planed after their arrival in this country. Here is one of the statements presented by the mayor of Vancouver from a Scandinavian emigrant station:
Mayor and Council of Vancouver:
Many hundreds of Scandinavians have lately arrived here, and we are glad to see them. But we admit it pains us often when young men and girls arrive without funds, no work, no friends, and not knowing the language. We try to find jobs for them, but with the city full of idle men, what chance has a newcomer? We find men among them who are educated. We find among them mechanics, chemists, musicians, almost starving. And this is what they tell us: that the government carries on propaganda in Norway, Sweden and Denmark, employing agents whose business is to induce as many as possible to migrate to Canada.
Now I, for one, do not believe that this government employs such agents. I rather think the railroads, together with the steamship companies, are the guilty ones, and they should be made to look after them when they get here.
In the meantime here they are, and more arriving almost daily. Would someone think of a plan to help these sturdy Norsemen, and be a big brother to them in their hour of need?

Just one more thing. If these companies persist in such methods of bringing in settlers we will consider ways and means by which we can counteract their propaganda, to wit: write a strong protest and explain in the publications of Europe the rotten methods employed by these people. Give us a square deal. Respectfully yours,
J. J. Petersen,
In charge.
Since the unemployment conference last tautumm the situation has grown steadily worse. X will not emulate the example of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and read the large numbers of letters which might be produced regarding this matter. I would simply indicate that from almost every industrial centre there have been sent in protests against the present policy. It will be remembered that- two years ago from my own city of Winnipeg there came a resolution which I placed on the order paper to this effect, in part:
And whereas a percentage in excess of 33$ per cent of persons under relief are returned soldiers, or persons with short residence in Manitoba, who might property be classed as "citizens of Canada at large", and that the relief of such persons should be borne by the country as a whole;
This clause calls attention to the fact that a considerable number of the people in Winnipeg who need help have recently arrived in the city.

And lastly, that this manifesto be translated into foreign languages and printed.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I submit that with the very large immigration from all parts of Great Britain and the continent, there are already a sufficient number of people in Canada to either make or break 4 pm. any immigration policy that the government may devise. If the people now here are not satisfied, and continue to write to .their home papers telling the actual conditions that prevail in Canada, it is almost hopeless, even with the expenditure by the government of enormous sums of money, to induce any more immigrants to come to this country. I notice, for instance, in the Daily Herald, the one labour daily which is printed in Great Britain, there occurs the following statement, in the issue of February 5:
Notices displayed outside employment exchanges in Britain declare that thousands Df men are wanted in Canada.
Why do the authorities lie to our unemployed?
The Canadian papers are full of reports of unemployment and suffering in that country.
Here are a few of the headlines from three recent issues of the "Evening Telegram," an important Toronto newspaper:-
"All types of men seek jobs. Veteran's badge isn't a help. Labor Bureau up against big task hundreds of applicants. Outsiders come to city: single men out of work suffer-some cases of near starvation."
"No food for four days. Man's pitiable plight. Sought work, not alms-fell exhausted at 'House of Industry' door."
"How 'Other Half' Lives. Told by mother. Distressed wife shows how furniture is broken up to keep
her children warm."

These headings are not taken from a Canadian Labour paper, nor from any paper that is confessedly out of sympathy with the government's immigration policy; they are taken from the files of the Evening Telegram of Toronto. We are already in such close touch with the Motherland that conditions here cannot continue to be unsatisfactory without their becoming very definitely known by. the Labour papers of the Old Country; and I would repeat, that conditions being so known, all the efforts the Canadian government officials overseas may put forth to induce immigration to Canada will be largely nullified.
The Department of Immigration has emphasized the statement that only farm labourers and domestic servants are being sought for in England or in Europe. At the unemployment conference the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), for years the Acting Minister of Immigration, stated:
The most careful scrutiny is made of entrants to Canada, and they are the agricultural class very largely.
Now, is this actually true? I notice a very interesting editorial in The Federated Railwayman of November, 1924, commenting upon this statement of the Minister of the Interior. That editorial contains a very enlightening table showing the emigration from Great Britain to Canada by occupations. With the permission of the House, I should like to place excerpts from this editorial and the table it contains on record in Hansard.
The document submitted is as follows:

Now I should like to ask: upon whom should the responsibility for these unemployed immigrants fall? First of all, should it fall upon the individual and his family? That is largely where it falls to-day. Mr. Speaker, I regard it as absolute cruelty to induce people to come here either by false statements or by statements that are not sufficiently understood by the intending emigrant, and then allow that man to be thrown out upon an overcrowded labour market. I do not suggest that the government deliberately makes false statements in inducing people to come here, and yet I know sufficient of English life and of the viewpoint of the ordinary Englishman to know that a great many of the statements that are made leave a very false impression. I hold in my hand one of the postern which is broadcast on the other side. In large type appear the words "Why Pay Rent? Why not own your own farm?" And there is a picture of quite a comfortable farm house. I do not think I need to go into this question very fully to show to hon. members that there are tens of thousands of farmers who have been a good many years out on the western prairies who do not own as comfortable a house as the one pictured. I know perfectly well, on the other hand, that there are hundreds of

Unemployed Immigrants
houses that are equally comfortable, and some much more comfortable than the one pictured. But the impression left is that any man may hare a house like this, and that he may secure it very readily.

Does the
advertisement indicate that there is a mortgage on that house?

speechtext:
No, nor does it
indicate that the vast proportion of the farms in the three prairie provinces are very heavily mortgaged. There is nothing said about that. The poster goes on:
The British and Canadian governments have arranged to advance funds for the settlement of farm workers and tenant farmers of limited means, and other suitable families who desire to engage in farming, on improved farms in Canada.
It states that there are farms ready for occupation within a reasonable distance of schools, railways and markets. I will leave the agricultural members of this House to say whether all these farms spoken of are within easy range of schools, railways and markets. If so, how is it that a large number of rural schools in my own province of Manitoba were closed last year? If so, how is it that bills for new railways were placed before this House last year? Surely this would indicate the necessity of bringing railways nearer to the homes of those already located?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: Might I ask the hon. member if this is one of the farms that the government is going to sell to these new settlers on twenty-five year terms, and easy rates of interest?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
I believe so. Another statement made is that loans repayable over twenty-five years, with interest at 5 per cent per annum can be secured. That is a better rate of interest than people already living here can secure. I do not know that I need go any further in reading this poster. My point is simply this: that although the statements may not be absolutely false, yet in the atmosphere in which they are published in England they convey an absolutely misleading idea as to the conditions that actually prevail in Canada, and we have large numbers of people coming over in response to such advertisements who are bitterly disappointed after they have been here for a short time.
I ask whether the individual should be allowed to bear the whole brunt of the unemployment, and permit me in this connection to quote one or two brief paragraphs from speakers who presented a case a few months ago before the mayor of the city of Montreal. This clipping is taken from the Montreal Daily Star of October 17, 1924:
A thorough review of the condition of unemployment in this city was given by H. B. Mackenzie, president Board of Trade; Geo. Lyman, chairman of the special committee, interviewing His Worship; J. T. Foster, president of the Trades and Labour Council; Right Rev. John Farthing, Bishop of Montreal; Lady Drummond, and several others. Mayor Duquette presented his views. He summed up by attacking the immigration policy of the country for allowing more men to come to Canada than could be absorbed in industry, and suggested that an embargo on the country's natural resources would help to promote manufacturing and give work.
In the course of that discussion I notice this appeal from J. Howard T. Falk, a prominent social worker in the city of Montreal:
You may leave the unemployed alone, but if they are left alone with their wives and children, you will have all the other problems crowding in, sickness, character breaking, wife desertion, non-support, delinquency, for which you will have to pay through the nose later on.
Undoubtedly, under modem conditions, the question of unemployment cannot be settled by the individual. There are admittedly shiftless individuals, and lazy individuals, and drunken individuals, but the great part of unemployment to-day is involuntary, and hence the state in some form cannot divest itself of certain responsibilities. I should say that one of the first responsibilities of the federal government here is to insist that there shall be a greater correlation between the work of its own officials and that of the officials of the several railway companies. The other day I asked several questions, which were passed as an order for return, as follows:
What salary was paid to the manager of the Colonization Department of the Canadian National Railways in Europe in the year 1924?
The reply came:
The management does not consider it in the public interest to publish this information.
I asked further:
What sum was paid to the manager as expenses, travelling and personal, in addition to this salary?
And the reply was:
The management does not consider it in the public interest to publish this information.
Here we have a very curious situation, Mr. Speaker. We have the Canadian National railways branching out into all kinds of sidelines, among others into an immigration policy, a policy upon which this House is by no means unanimous, a policy which may very easily lead to duplication of effort on the part of the Colonization department of the railways and the government's own agents; and yet when we ask what are the salaries and the expenses connected with those departments of the railway's operations we are told that the management "does not consider it in the public interest to publish this information." As a

Unemployed, Immigrants

member of this House I protest against this view of the matter. I urge that it is decidedly "in the public interest" that we should know how much money is being spent by the Canadian National. It is of very little use scrutinizing the expenses of our own departments, very little use deciding what policy we shall follow, when any policy we determine upon may be overridden and much larger amounts spent by a board over which we have no control. I submit that the position taken by the Minister of Hallways (Mr. Graham) the other day is quite indefensible. He laid it down as the policy of the government that this House should not interfere with the details of railway management. I submit that this is not one of the details of railway management. If the railway company embarks upon an immigration policy it seems to me it is high time we should understand that such a matter in all its details should come under the purview of this House.
It is not my purpose to go into any detail in considering what part of the responsibility for unemployment should be borne by the municipal, by the provincial, or by the federal authorities. That ought to be a matter of arrangement. But there are two factors which are very largely responsible for unemployment. First, financial policy of the government, and second, immigration. Perhaps, after the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) the other day, I should add, ocean freight rates-I am not going into that matter. But in any case the federal government is definitely responsible for all these three. Under these conditions it is absolutely unfair to unload on the provinces or on the municipalities, the responsibility for immigrants who are unemployed shortly after their arrival in this country.
Why should the government refuse to accept responsibility for the effects of its own policies? That is a question which ought to be answered. If the government accept my motion it seems to me they would be simply showing their sincerity and good faith by admitting that if we bring people to this country, and those people are out of work within two years, the least we can do is to take care of them. I would not venture to suggest what form this care should take. Personally I think we might very well hold the railway companies responsible for that care, because even more than the federal government the railways are responsible for the propaganda that brings these immigrants here. In any case the responsibility for these new immigrants who are unemployed is placed directly with the government.

At the present time and for some time past we have had this question of unemployment tossed backward and forward between the provincial and federal authorities, and in the meantime the people themselves have suffered and are suffering to-day. I wish we in this House could sometimes get away- I have said it before now-from our statistics and from our thought of general policies, to picture to ourselves what unemployment really means-the discouraged men and the broken home, the under-privileged and in many cases under-nourished children. Surely we cannot go on indifferent to matters of this kind. So I would ask that even if the government are determined that the general matter of unemployment is not a federal concern; even if they are determined-and I do not acquiesce at all in that point of view-that they will not give relief but will leave that all to the provinces, I would urge that the least the government can do is to assume this little bit of the unemployment responsibility and care for the immigrants for two years after their arrival in this country.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that we need a larger population in Canada. There is a class of people that I know would be willing to come back to Canada if they could afford to do so; I refer to our Canadian-born who are now in the United States. These people would not require to be maintained or supported by the Dominion government, by the provincial government or by any cities or municipalities. Since 1911 a great many of our Canadian people have gone to the United States in the hope of finding better conditions, but I am informed that after a few years' experience in that country they would be willing to return if the conditions were favourable. I am aware that the federal government have done a good deal to try to get these people to come back, but I would urge upon the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Robb) that he renew his efforts in that direction. Those of our Canadians who are willing to come back from the United States are familiar with our laws, usages and customs; they have had the experience of earning their living in this country. They are fishermen, farmers' sons, men who have worked in the woods or in saw mills, and this class of men will not be a burden to the country.
It is not my intention to make any extended remarks on this subject, but I submit this is the class of people we should first look after. If immigrants from foreign

Unemployed Immigrants
countries prove to be a burden then I hope we will not have too many. On the other hand I understand that the government has lately been making a careful choice of the immigrants coming into Canada, and I must congratulate them upon taking that step. In the past there has been a tendency to allow people to come into this country who could not become good Canadian citizens. I hope the minister will see to it that larger numbers of our Canadians who went to the United States will come back to Canada in the near future.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
What inducements, does my
hon. friend suggest, should be held out to the Canadians who have gone to the States?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS

Whatever money we
would spend to bring foreigners to this country, we should first spend to bring our Canadian-born back from the United States.
Mr. SPENCER; In what way would the hon. member have the money spent?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: In different ways. In the first place I would suggest that their travelling expenses back to Canada should be paid. These people should be induced to go on the farms and not to the cities. In order to induce them to go on the farms we should adopt the policy of the province of Quebec where the government has to-day opened up the forest for settlers. The government is opening up little farms, putting up small houses, _ building bams, and clearing a few acres of land. They invite these people to come and settle down in the province. A part of that forest which has been opened to the settlers possesses a valuable resource in the form of lumber. A settler full of health and ambition is not afraid to go into the forest, chop down trees which he can sell as pulpwood or for manufacture into pulp, lumber or other products. The policy adopted in Quebec gives a great inducement to these men to come there. In the last few months this policy has been made known to a great many Canadian subjects who are now in the United States, and many of these people have accepted the invitation of the province and have come back to their homeland, and are good settlers.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
If there is any one phase of immigration that this government and the preceding government has carried on with energy, it has been the attempt to repatriate the French Canadian. If that policy has not succeeded up to the present time, I do not think there can be 91 i
very much hope for success in the future. In the last ten years large sums of money have been spent to encourage colonization. Many people, mostly ecclesiastics, have gone to the New England states in order to personally endeavour to persuade those who have left Quebec to come back. They have offered them all kinds of inducements in the shape of farms in the province of Ontario and other places. If all these endeavours have not brought results, I do not think there can be very much hope for that particular kind of immigration in the future. My hon. friend from Restigouche and Madawaska (Mr. Michaud) says they are coming back and glad to get back, and that the province of Quebec is providing ready-made farms for them. My information is that they are not coming back in very large numbers, and judging from the statement of my hon. friend, they cannot afford to come back; they must have their fares paid. Perhaps they will ask for a return ticket. In that case they might come back, have a holiday in the village, and if they did not like it any better they could go away again.

speechtext:
With reference to the
settlers who come back to Canada, not only to the province of Quebec, but also to the province of New Brunswick, where I live, I would suggest that their travelling expenses1 should be paid, and they should not have * return ticket. They never had any return tickets, I am informed, and the suggestions from my hon. friends are not called for.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
This resolution presented
by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) is to my mind a most extraordinary proposal. I think we must assume that he anticipates unemployment as a permanent condition in Canada. He does not see any hope of relief from unemployment. He does not foresee a time when the people of Canada will all be employed. I know that there will always be some unemployment, but evidently my hon. friend anticipates that the condition that exists at the present time must be provided for by legislation continuously. I would be very sorry to have such an idea as that about our country. The conditions would be desperate indeed if we had at this time to provide for the maintenance of men who come into this country at least during the first three years of their residence here.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Are there not already arrangements that an immigrant who is unsuitable in certain respects may be returned by the transportation company? And are there
Unemployed Immigrants

not- also provisions that the immigrant, no matter how long he is in this country, who labours under certain difficulties, may be deported at the will of the Immigration department? It is not a new idea that an indigent immigrant should be cared for.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
I think the maintenance of every person who comes into this country and does not get employment for two years is a new thing, and would have an effect which my hon. friend does not anticipate. Why should not the native-born citizen who cannot get work be maintained? Why should the man who has just come here be supported by the state because he cannot get work, and the man who is born in this country and unable to find work be compelled to make a living by some other means? Such an arrangement would discriminate against the native-born. Perhaps a little more may be expected of the men born in this country, but I do not think a solution for the unemployment is to be found in the direction my hon. friend suggests, and I do not think his resolution could be put into effect. I want to give my hon. friend credit for the motives which prompt him to make his proposal. I think we all have the deepest sympathy for the man who is willing to work and unable to find work. Perhaps those who have been through that experience would have more sympathy than any others. But, it is a desperate state of affairs for a man and for his family, when he is strong, willing and able to work, yet cannot find employment. What I think is needed, Mr. Speaker, in a new country like Canada is a national policy that will provide work instead of paying doles in the shape of maintenance. I hope the time will never come in Canada when we will pay doles, and certainly to begin now and take a considerable sum of money annually from the federal treasury to maintain men who are out of work-and I submit it could not be confined to men who have just entered the country

would create an additional tax upon industry; and thus still further depress conditions and postpone the day when there will be employment for all the citizens of Canada. This government has refused to accept any responsibility fqr unemployment. They will not relieve distress. They say that is the burden of the municipalities. When the unemployed march down here from Toronto and make their request, this government says, "We cannot do anything. Here is the British North America Act. If you can get anything out of that, why, feed on it, but we will take no further responsibility. That must come IMr. Woodsworth.]
from the municipalities and private charities." Of course, private charity means that these men are put in the position of mendicants, and that is most dangerous for this or any other country. The development of the mendicant spirit is one of the bad features of the dole system, and I hope the time will not come in this country when men will be able to look forward to maintenance whether they work or not. You keep a man who is unable to obtain employment for a certain period until he loses more or less all his selfrespect, then he is willing to take dole for the rest of his natural life. A trade policy such as we have to-day in Canada, which closes factories, produces the unemployment that exists in Canada. It is not so much the reduction of duties, not so much what is being done, as the threat of what is going to be done; with responsible ministers standing in their place and telling us that this is "the death knell of protection."

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: Terrible!

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
It is terrible. My hon.
friend may use that word seriously, because the effect of it is to prevent capital from opening up new . avenues of employment. Nothing can be worse in this country than that. What was the effect of the declarations from the other side of the House during last session? It was the curtailment of many extensions that otherwise would have taken place. It made capital fearful, and it has prevented many from going on with enterprises because they did not know wbat next would come from this government's policy.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Presuming that my hon.
friend's statement is correct, would the assurance of the Prime Minister, given, I think, at Toronto, that there was going to be no further interference with the'tariff, not somewhat abate the feeling which my hon. friend suggests?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
I might remind my hon.
friend that in 1919 the Prime Minister adopted a platform for his party or his party adopted a platform for him. Immediately afterwards, he went around this country telling the leaders of industry that that did not matter at all; that they were not going to put it into effect. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) stated that on the floor of this House. While that stood, things were not so bad in this country. My hon. friend will remember that, following the platform which was -adopted in 1919 declaring for free trade, assurances were given that free trade would not be introduced; that the manufac-

Unemployed Immigrants
rimers would be perfectly satisfied. Following that again came the reduction and the threats that were made by the different ministers of the crown. After those threats were made, unemployment began to be serious in Canada. That unemployment has continued, and I am afraid it will continue. What is worse than men being brought out here who find themselves unemployed for a period, is the fact that tens of thousands, yes, hundreds of thousands of the native-born of this country, people bom here, educated here, who have learned a trade or profession, by the time they are ready to work, have to go over the border to get employment. Conditions in Canada to-day are just what they were in 1876, 1877 and 1878.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Are they not somewhat
similar to what they were in 1913 before this government began to tinker with the tariff?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: If my hon. friend lived in a city, in any centre of population, he would know that would be a perfectly silly question to ask. Unemployment in 1913 was not a fraction of what it is to-day, and unemployment that existed in 1913 was due to a depression in the United States as much as to any depression in Canada. That depression began over there, but what is happening now is that our neighbours are prosperous while we are in a state of depression.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
My hon. friend speaks
about unemployment in 1912 and 1913 being less severe than it is at the present time. The winter of 1912-13 was the only time when we had bread lines in the province from which I come.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: In 1912-13, I was personally responsible for the relief of anything in the shape of unemployment in one of the principal cities in this country. I was as close up against it as I am to my friend here, the hon. member for Strathcona (Mr. Warner), and I can assure my hon. friend that there was nothing at all to be compared with conditions that exist to-day. We had no bread lines in the city of Toronto. The House of Industry was not spending more than twenty-five per cent of what it is spending to-day in the relief of distress. We did not have missions throughout the city as there are today providing soup and meals for the unemployed and those who are hungry. There is one there conducted by a French-Canadian evangelist where they are feeding from one to three hundred men every night. That is going on now.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: Did you have any donations from Russia in 1913 for the unemployed?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: I cannot recall any donations from Russia in 1913, but I can assure my hon. friend that conditions in 1913 are not to be compared with conditions to-day. Conditions to-day are twenty, yes a huhdred, times worse than they were then.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
My hon. friend suggests that
serious threats on this citadel of protection were the cause of much unemployment. I should like to know, as a matter of interest, where these serious threats came from.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
The first one came from
the Prime Minister himself, but the most striking one came from the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart). Then we had a very elegantly phrased one from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell).

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend really
take them seriously?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
It would not matter so
much about my taking them so seriously, but capital generally has taken them seriously. That is the point to which I direct the attention of the House. Almost from the day that these threats were made from that side of the House, there has been a tightening up of capital, a curtailment of industry and an increase of unemployment. My hon. friends may smite, but there is the fact and it cannot be controverted. Conditions to-day are worse than they have been in this Dominion to my knowledge since 1876.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
I will take
issue with my hon. friend there. I think my hon. friend was living in Toronto in 1891, 1892 and 1893, and he will remember if he thinks back, the procession of workmen carrying the black flag. He will also remember that a great portion of the city of Toronto, a very large portion of Parkdale was uninhabited at all. If conditions are as bad in Toronto today, I would like to know it.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
My hon. friend has raised a question that needs some explanation. He tells about the hard times that existed in Toronto in 1891. I can tell him the reasons very largely for that. From 1885 to 1890 there had been the wildest and craziest land speculation boom that ever took place in any part of this Dominion. By 1891 the bubble burst, and men who thought they were worth half a million or a million dollars were in poverty. When they had to meet their covenants they were completely insolvent.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: I can explain and describe it to my hon. friend. I remember 1891 and the processions that took place then were composed of, perhaps, a hundred or a hundred and fifty persons.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: No.

speechtext:
I cannot remember any
very large one. I will tell my hon. friend something else. The man who organized those processions under the black flag was offered a position to work on the building of the city hall. He would not take the work, and when that fact was published, we had no more carrying of black flags or processions. I happen to know that because at that time I was a reporter of the city hall, and it was my duty to describe those processions, to go over all the facts as to who organized them, what they were for and all the rest of it. They were organized by two or three men who did not want to work. That is proved by the tact that when work was offered they would not take it.

Order. The
hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) is supposed to have the floor.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: Thank you.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
I have no more to say
than this, that instead of the government preparing to pay out doles to men out of work it is the duty of parliament to provide work. I do not gather from that poster that men are being brought in to go .into the cities; those who come in response to the poster are coming to do farming. And that is the best kind of immigration we can have, because we have lots of land in Ontario, thousands of farms that can be purchased for very much less than they are worth, including the buildings on them. This is due to the fact that the farmers have grown old and their children have gone away, so that they are unable any longer to work the land. There are thousands of farms in Ontario in that state which can be purchased for a great deal less than they are really worth, and these would be ideal places for immigrants to settle in. I say therefore that it is the duty of the government to make such arrangements as will make it possible for these men coming out with a knowledge of agriculture to go on the farms of Ontario. But I am opposed to any principle of paying maintenance money to men who come to this country. It is better a thousand times for the government to enter upon some extensive works to give them employment than to begin to turn them against work as soon as they get here.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
I did
not intend to speak in this debate but a few remarks have been made upon which I feel obliged to make some observations. I recognize the sincerity of the mover of this resolution and I know that he wishes well in regard to this great question of unemployment. I have also listened to the remarks of the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken), and I must say that I always feel disappointed that, in these trying times when so many difficult questions face us and when conditions are so troublesome, our friends to the right,

Unemployed Immigrants
whose ability I would not question for a moment, have no other solution to offer us than the one panacea of higher protection.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
What solution do you
offer?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: Perhaps I should admit that I have no great solution to offer.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: Then why criticize us?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Have patience. I do not feel called upon to propose any solution irrespective of whether or not I am sure it is going to benefit us, simply because it happens to be the god that I have always worshipped in days gone by. As regards the steamship companies, I have a little experience gained a number of years ago in the way of getting immigration into Canada. I do not know what system the government follows, but I do think that if the Canadian government has an agent associated with any steamship company it should discontinue that policy. The government cannot interfere or find fault with propaganda issued by the steamship companies, but if there is a steamship company's agent who is also an agent for the Canadian government, then the government has some responsibility in the matter. The government has a responsibility so far as immigrants are concerned after they have come to Canadia, but the steamship companies have none; consequently the companies want nothing but a certain amount of passenger traffic to make their business a paying proposition.
In connection with the class of immigrants that come to the country, we have heard a good deal about unemployment, and I take it that we all agree that this is deplorable. No one cares to hear of destitution or hard times or suffering on the part of women and children, or of men, for that matter. And we are up against a situation that calls for the most serious consideration. To begin with, ours is a large country, one that has room for an immense population. The country is traversed by railways; and as I mentioned not long ago our -house in Canada is too large for us; its furnishings are too expensive and we cannot pay the rent. That is the condition we are in to-day. Are we going to sit idly by and do nothing? There is unemployment in Toronto, in Winnipeg and in the other larger cities, and are we to sit down and do nothing to provide work for these people, at the same time getting more immigrants into the country? I would point out that there has never been unemployment in the agricultural districts of Canada.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: Will the hon. member mention any time in the history of this country when there was no unemployment in the large cities?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: I was going to say a few words on that.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: Is it not true that a very large number of the unemployed in the cities during the winter have been employed out on the farms in the summer until the land was frozen? Do they not work up to the harvest and then drift to the cities?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
That may be true to some extent, but I do not think that things are always what they are made out to be in this regard. I can only speak for one province, where I know men have been able to get good wages all summer. They have a large amount of money when the cold weather comes and they drift into the cities, and owing to the attractions of city life that money soon disappears after they -have got there. They then become a burden on the city.
A good deal has been said about the industrial system, and it is my belief that its operations are responsible for a large amount of unemployment in Canada. If you foster industry by artificial means you are likely to have unemployment; if you could make all the factories of Canada really prosperous by such means, so that you could have more of them established, I believe the same question of unemployment would come up again. Let me tell the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) that the question is not one of production but of consumption. Canada can produce twice as much as the people of Canada can buy to-day. But under our present system we are unable to compete in the outside markets anywhere with our industrial products and consequently we must look to the home market to dispose of them. Our industries have been developed to such an extent that they can produce much more than the people can buy, and therefore the unemployment situation is inevitable. It is a vicious circle; however I have no doubt that my hon. friend from West Toronto is sincere in his belief that, if protection were given all these industries, the people would immediately be in a position to buy all that was produced.	t

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: We are buying too much from the United States.

speechtext:
I do not say they are buying too much. People are buying what they can afford to buy. The buying power of the

people, more especially of the agricultural community, has been reduced to such an extent that they are unable to purchase the goods they would purchase if conditions had been as prosperous as they had reason to expect. I claim, Mr. Speaker, that the great problem

it has been repeated again and again in this House, and it cannot be repeated too often-the great problem we have to-day is an agricultural problem, and that when we have solved it we Shall find that our industrial problem will be to a large extent solved as well. My hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) says that we buy too much from the United States. Again I come back to the question-of course I know some of the arguments that will be advanced-why is it we cannot get Canadian goods that we are so anxious and willing to purchase? Why is it they cost so much more than similar goods coming from the United States? There must be some reason, and one is that Canada has been made one of the dearest countries of the world in which to live in. Consequently you find the cost of production gets so high that the product cannot be sold to compete with the similar product of other countries.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Will the hon. member
explain why goods are so cheap in the States?

speechtext: -a more highly protected country?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: My friends always get back to that cry, "A more highly protected country." The idea that is being promulgated in t'he States at the present time is, "America for the Americans." They are getting tired of Europe and all its troubles, and they are going to build a ring around the United States of America and protect agriculture, they are going to bring everything up to a certain level and forget all about the troubles and miseries of the outside world while they live in complete happiness themselves. Now, Mr. Speaker, that is not such a dream as it may appear to be on the surface.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS

My right hon. friend says, "hear, hear." Such a policy may be possible in the United States, a country of immense distances and possessing a climate so varied that the soil is capable of producing everything necessary for the life of mankind even under the advanced civilization of to-day. But what are the circumstances in Canada? We are a debtor nation, we have a large indebtedness to Great Britain and other foreign countries-
[Me. Forke.]

speechtext:

That is a slip of the tongue. My hon. friend from West Toronto will never have to blaane me for lack of love of my Motherland. But the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meigben) in the course of his speech on the Address pointed out that we had interest to pay to Great Britain and foreign countries to the amount of $300,000000. How are we going to pay that immense sum every year unless we are able to sell our products to other countries? Now, 5 p.m. the United States is in an entirely different position; and when you begin to compare Canada with the United States the comparison is useless because the conditions are not parallel. A policy that would work well in the United States would be entirely unworkable in the Dominion.
But I am getting away a little from what I intended to say. There are two sides to this question, and I should like to meet them fairly and squarely. I am just as anxious as the hon. member for West Toronto not to see any unemployment, any hard times, but to have everyone prosperous and happy in this Dominion. I think we are all agreed upon that. The only trouble is, we cannot see eye to eye as to what remedy should be applied to bring about this desirable state of affairs.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: Will my hon. friend explain how the United States ceased to be a debtor nation? He will admit that not many years ago it was not a creditor nation.

speechtext:
They were out of debt

speechtext:
Even supposing they were,
their soil produces almost everything that its people require. The United States is not in the same position as Canada is to-day.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: It is.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
They are the largest free
trade area in the world.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
They are no bigger than we are. We are just as big.

Unemployed Immigrants

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: We are in an entirely different position.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS

people.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: If each state had been independent and had erected a tariff wall against its neighbour, does my right hon. friend say that the United States would be as prosperous a country as it is to-day?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: Such a thing would be nonsense. Why in the world would, a country have a tariff within its own borders? It does not matter where the business is done so long as it is done. The difference would be this, there would be a wider distribution of what the United States now has over the different states, but it would be accompanied by some expense, and I do not think it would be wise. If the hon. member will give us what the United States has we will be satisfied.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
I do not exactly follow my
right hon. friend's argument.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: Give us the kind of "free trade" they have and we will be satisfied.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
They have free trade among
themselves,-

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: So have we.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: -and if we were in exactly the same position probably we could get along as well as they have done, although I do not think their prosperity has come from protective principles-I do not admit it for one moment. There are a great many other reasons why the United States should be so prosperous without going into the field of protection.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
There is one disciple

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
My right
hon. friend is aware that last Saturday morning there appeared in the newspapers a statement that the American steel industry have had the worst year in the past five years; and they are a highly protected industry.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
How does that compare
with Nova Scotia?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: We will have sufficient time later to discuss free trade versus protection, or low versus high tariffs. In fact I do not think the subject would have been introduced so largely had it not been for my hon. friend from West Toronto, whose favourite theme protection seems to be. I have no doubt he sincerely believes that all our troubles today follow from the so-called low tariff now in force. It is simply a difference of opinion, and I hope some day my hon. friend will get more light upon the subject.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
We have a vast country sparsely settled, and yet we have unemployment. We are all anxiously seeking for the light. Listening to the stories which the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) has recited to the House, I have no doubt they are true. But only last night I picked up an Old Country newspaper in which I read a letter written by a family in Toronto to friends in Berwickshire,, saying, "We have been out in this new country just twelve months, and we are very happy." Only recently I read in another Old Country paper a speech made by a farmer from Alberta while visiting a town in Berwickshire in which he painted a most glowing picture of the prosperity of the Alberta farmer. I have no doubt that what he said was true in his particular case. At the same time-and I have mentioned this before-I have heard stories of destitution and want on the western prairies, and I also have no doubt that those stories unfortunately are true. I am perfectly certain that two members from the western provinces could tell directly opposite stories of conditions in their respective districts and both would be speaking .the truth. This is a fact which no one oan deny. Circumstances during the years which are past and gone have been not what they ought to have been in this country. But, Mr. Speaker I do believe that we have reached the point where if we get the proper dass of immigrants and proper conditions we are going to see better times so far as agriculture is concerned. I also realize that the government has no right to bring more immigrants into the country unless they are prepared to find places for them on their arrival.
I am not so sure about the federal government not being responsible for unemployment. So long as it pursues what may be termed a vigorous immigration policy I question very much as a matter of equity and justice whether it is right in asserting that it has nothing to do with unemployment. Were no new people being poured into the provinces under a federal immigration policy, I think the provincial and municipal authorities would be entirely responsible and would have to look after those unfortunate people who are out of work. I merely make this remark in passing.
I have watched the whole process of immigration into a new country, and no matter under what circumstances the immigration is
Unemployed Immigrants

conducted you will always find pathos and humour and tragedy in the immigration of a people into a new land, I would urge upon the government that the greatest of care should be taken in the handling of the immigrants immediately after they have landed upon the shores of Canada, and to see that they get located where they can earn a living.
I was rather astonished at the figures given by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr Woodsworth) showing that only about one-third of the male immigrants to this country belong to the agricultural class. I am sorry to hear that, because I do believe that immigrants who are unfitted for agricultural work are going to be a liability on this country for a good many years to come, if they come here m any large numbers. I am perfectly aware of the fact that a good many immigrants who were quite unacquainted with agriculture have come to this country, and have in the long run made good; but these are the exceptions and not the rule. So I would like to see great, care taken in the placing of the immigrants after they come to our shores.
But we shall never solve this question until we have made agriculture prosperous, until we have established an equilibrium between the wages paid in agriculture and the wages paid in other callings; the wages should be on a parity. We sometimes hear about the high wages that are paid to agricultural labourers, but, Mr. Speaker, I am one of those who believe that agricultural labourers are not paid high enough wages; and that is the trouble. We speak about farm labourers, and sometimes the phrase is used as if farm "labourers" were not of the very highest order. But m these modem times the farm labourer on the modern farm, if he is efficient, must be a man of intelligence, he must have some ability m the handling of machinery, and be a fairly good all-round man. I think an efficient farm servant is entitled to be well paid. But conditions have been such in farming as not to allow the wages to be paid which ought to be paid for what might be called efficient farm help. If we could put farming upon a paying basis with other industries, then I think a great many of our difficulties would be solved.
Why do people leave the farm and go to the cities to swell the ranks of the unemployed? It is because there are periodically boom times in the cities, and because wages are higher there for the time being, and consequently the young men and the young women on the farms become dissatisfied and go to the cities. Then a slack time comes, and we have the whole stoiy of unemployment

over and over again. That brings me back to where I began. We shall never solve this question of unemployment until we have made the farm an attractive place to live, and until the remuneration there is equal to the industry and energy expended on the farm. I know a great many people think that agricultural people are selfish in always advocating this as a remedy for our difficulties in Canada; but I do not advocate it for a single minute from a selfish point of view; I do it because I honestly believe this is the solution of our problem.
I have repeated again and again in this House that I have no quarrel with our industrial people. I would like to see the factories in this country prosperous. I am just as sorry as the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) to see people idle in Toronto or in other manufacturing cities. But we should realize that the system we are fpllow-ing is economically unsound, and that to preach a little higher protection will never solve our problem. I want to tell the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) that I am very much disappointed in him that, with his great ability he does nothing more to help us out of our difficulties than to preach this one doctrine of high protection.
