I believe that it is quite right to get immigrants provided they are of the right class, and provided they reach the places where they can earn a living. And that will not be in the city of Toronto or in any other large centre of population. A small percentage, of course, can always be absorbed in the great cities, but I believe that those who are there now should first be taken care of before we get more in to swell the popu-

Unemployed Immigrants
lation of our cities. One of the great problems of modern times is the continual drift of population from the rural districts into our large cities. And how can this be stopped? I do _ not know- I only hope that under modern conditions of life in the rural districts, where we have now the car, the telephone, radio, and easier communication with the great centres, rural life will become more and more attractive and people will stay on the farm. That would help to solve our difficulties.
In conclusion, my heart and sympathy are with the new immigrant, because I know just about how he feels when he plants his foot on an unknown shore.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this problem of wages
seems to be one of the biggest problems that we have to grapple with to-day. If we were to follow the advice of our friends to the right, we would boost our industries and keep them running full time, and thereby get rid of the problem of unemployment; but I fail to see any sound reasoning in that suggestion. Provided that industry prospers, as my leader (Mr. Forke) has said, industry adds to industry, and under the system of protection of our industries, organized labour and organized capital are able to demand the rate of return that each of them wants for the service it performs. Then when in addition we add interest on the capital invested, what is the position in which we find ourselves? We find that the man who is working where he has not the benefit of organized labour drifts to the place where he will get big wages. This drains not only the rural communities, but other countries as well where the wages are lower. I fail to see how-even if you had a tariff so high that it would prohibit everything coming in, and prohibit men drifting to the places where conditions were not advantageous to the worker-you can prevent unemployment even if you give protection to the limit and develop industry to the limit.
I listened with interest to the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) advocating the cause of the worker. I have as much sympathy with the worker perhaps as any man in this House. I have be.en a worker practically all my life, and at manual labour, I might say. I have studied tihe prevailing conditions in this country. The hon. member for Centre Winnipeg referred to a poster that was being broadcast in the old land advertising conditions in Canada. I have employed help myself, and as he showed that poster my mind went back to the nineties when times were rather hard on the farm as
well as in industry in Ontario. I remember hiring a man, at that time, twenty-one years of age, and without a dollar in his pocket. He worked five years on our farm, three years for my father, and two for myself. That man to-day owns his home, and it is the equal of the one described in that poster. He has paid for his home, for his stock, chattels, farm and everything. And he did it all by honest labour; he has played the part of a good citizen. I will cite some other cases. It was my privilege some years ago to go to Onoway in the province of Alberta, about forty miles northwest of Edmonton. I had occasion to go ten miles from Onoway, out into a section where the roads were not built at that time, and what did I find when I got there? I found a man from the centre of London, England, who had hewn out a home for himself in that place. He had good buildings, a comfortable home, and he was clerk of the municipality.
I was more than astonished that a man of his intelligence should pass over so much of this vast country and go to such an undesirable section to settle. I have another case in mind, that of a man with whom I am very intimately acquainted, who came from the heart of London at sixteen years of age in those early nineties; came to our section of the country where work was very hard to get even in the rural sections. In those days he worked at fifty cents a day or whatever he could get. To-day he has just as nice a farm as the one described in the poster that has been referred to. He went home, by the way, the early part of this winter on a visit to England. That man never got a dollar that he did not earn by his own hard work, yet when he came here, as he said himself, he did not know how to put a set of whiffle-trees together.
I claim, as someone has already remarked in this debate, that land is just as cheap in the older parts of Ontario as it is anywhere else in Canada, when we consider the value of the improvements. We have free-grant land to-day in Ontario in close proximity to churches, schools, railways, markets and everything else. Why is it, therefore, that men are going to the cities? Organized labour has made certain demands. They will work only eight hours a day and at a certain rate; they will only do so much work for so much money. The farmer has to compete in the markets of the world, and he has to work longer hours and harder for less pay. Last session, a little less than a year ago, there was a strike of letter carriers in the city of Toronto. They were then getting about $1,500 a year,
Unemployed Immigrants

while mail carriers in the rural sections were getting only S600 a year,, and at that time we were endeavouring to get a little more for them. In other words, the man in the city was getting two and a half times as much as the man in the country. Now why is that? Why is it that wages are high in the city while in the country even the government persists in paying men less than they pay those who work in the cities? That is a thing I cannot understand. Until these wages are made more uniform by the government and by everybody concerned, the drift cityward will continue and we will have unemployment. If wages were made lower in the city, in the governmental departments-even in the civil service-results would be beneficial so far as the movement to the city is concerned. Those in the civil service think they are not getting enough, but I claim that if the salaries paid by the government were lowered a little bit you would find less of a stampede from the rural sections and you would not have the competition of the bright, brainy boys and girls from the country who come into the cities and take up some of the best positions in the gift of the government. Moreover, many of those who love fanning would stay on the farm; they now come to the city because of the mere pittance they get for their labours in the country. We want to make the conditions more difficult in the cities; we want to make them less attractive. Remuneration for work in the country must be made at least equal to wages paid in the city, otherwise we cannot hope to hold our people on the farms; we cannot hope to have a prosperous country or accomplish all that we should accomplish. It is right that industries should prosper, but they can only go so far when they have to call a halt and the agricultural sections of the country have to take the lead. So I say that if we are to have any real national prosperity we will have to bring about a reversal of the present conditions; those engaged in agriculture will have to get a- little more for their labour, and employment in the cities will have to be made a little less attractive.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Fort William and Rainy River):
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, allow me first to say that I believe the hon. member who introduced the resolution (Mr. Woodsworth) is sincere in doing so and that undoubtedly he shows a very great interest in the working men of this country. Though I cannot agree with some of his conclusions, at the same time I am sure he deserves the gratitude of the unemployed in this country for the interest he 
takes on their behalf. I cannot support the resolution myself, because I can hardly see how you could provide a living for unemployed immigrants while you allowed our own Canadian unemployed to go without similar assistance. Practically the same argument was put up by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) who spoke a little while ago. However, the resolution does bring before the House and the country the present conditions in Canada and shows the need for deep thought on the part of us all with regard to the solving of the problem.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: There is this difference: that the native-born Canadian who is unemployed can go to the United States, but the poor fellow who is an immigrant cannot get through.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Well, unfortunately, in
addition to the Canadian-born people who are going to the United States I happen to know that a number of the others are going also; they are both going out of the country at the present time.
It is rather interesting to sit here this afternoon and listen to various hon. members in different parts of the House describe the conditions as they exist in Canada. When my right hon. leader (Mr. Meighen), in moderate terms, described those conditions he was accused of being nothing but a pessimist; and when in my remarks on the Address I took the same attitude, pointed out exactly the conditions which we all know to exist, many of the Liberal papers and a number of Liberal speakers accused me of simply talking pessimism. But the country generally knows that these conditions exist and is crying for some remedy.
I consider the conditions worse than they have ever been so far back as my memory goes, and I have been taking an interest in business affairs in Canada, in the conditions of unemployment and business generally, for at least twenty-five years. I certainly have never known the conditions to equal those in Canada at present-the conditions of unemployment, of depression, and of exodus from the country. The very fact that last year, in, October, a month when business and employment are usually at their best, fifty mayors of Ontario waited upon the provincial premier asking him for help on account of the unemployment or the threatened unemployment for the ensuing winter-that is something that never occurred before in the history of Canada so far as my memory carries me, and even so far as my knowledge of history carries me. So there is no doubt

Unemployed Immigrants
that unemployment conditions are severe. There is also no doubt that there is no use bringing into this country labourers, at any rate of the ordinary Kind, labourers who intend to work in the cities, to take up employment in industrial plants. It is true we may still continue to bring in-and I think we should do so-as many of those who are willing to go upon farms as it is possible to bring in and as it is possible to place upon the land.
May I say in regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Restigouche and Madawaska (Mr. Michaud) as to the bringing back to this country of the French Canadians who have gone to the United States, that I at least- and I believe I speak for the larger number of Canadians-would be only too happy to see those French Canadians who left the country brought back once more to take their place as good and useful citizens of this country.
But at the present time there is no use in attempting it, because there is no work for them any more than there is work for any other labourers who wish to come back. So far as it is possible to put them on the land they certainly should be brought back, but there is no use at the present time bringing into the industrial centres of the country either French Canadians or any other class of people who cannot get work, and who would consequently have to join, the ranks of the unemployed.
What a tragedy it is, when one considers the -immense area of the country;-Canada has an area greater than that of the United States, a country with a population of a hundred and ten million, Canada has twice the area of the whole of Europe, if you leave out Russia, yet in that part of Europe there are three hundred millon people; and we have in double the area only nine million people! And when you consider all our magnificent resources, our millions of acres of' fertile land and all the other resources of which we speak, what a tragedy it is that to-day, in this House of Commons of Canada, we are debating what can be done for the unemployed1-for that is the basis of the resolution. It is certainly a terrible condition, in a new country with such possibilities and such potentialities, to be spending the time of the House of Commons wondering how we can help the terrible conditions of unemployment that exist. In spite of the criticisms of my hon. friend the member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) and the other hon. members who take the same attitude, I submit, after serious thought, that the chief cause of the depressed industrial conditions in our country is the
unstable tariff policy of the government. I submit that that is the chief cause of the depression in the cities. I do not contend it is causing depression in the prairie provinces. I go so far as to admit that in the prairie provinces they have very good reason, from their individual and sectional standpoint, for arguing for a lower tariff. There is no doubt they would gain to a certain extent, temporarily at least, under lower tariff. But there is also no doubt that in the industrial centres of the country, in cities such as Toronto, Hamilton, Peterborough, Galt and Paris in the provinces of Ontario, and Sherbrooke, Montreal, Three Rivers, Quebec and other cities in the province of Quebec, they absolutely require protection in order to carry on their industries. And there is no doubt that the farmers surrounding those cities absolutely need protection for the cities for the maintenance of the home market of which the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke), the leader of the Progressive party, spoke a few moments ago. If you have not protection for the industries you simply allow the cheap labour of a Europe and the low standards of living of a Europe to be imported into Canada. Without that proper protection you cannot keep out their goods.

speechtext: Just another question-

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
We not only import the
goods we produce in this country, but we import a lot we do not produce. This government in the past negotiated a trade treaty with France, and in that trade treaty we have lowered the tariff, for example, on a lot of luxuries. We are being paid by importing a greater amount of luxuries into Canada for the goods we export to France. But as to the goods we can produce in this country, lines of production in which our industries have been developed, I submit, it is far better
Unemployed Immigrants

to have a little more expensive article if necessary and keep our own people employed, than to force them to go to the United States, the most highly protected country in the world, to earn a living. That is what I believe is necessary-we must have a stable tariff policy. As the hon. member for West Toronto said, it has not been so much the cuts in the tariff, but the continual threatening of cuts, although the cuts of course have done harm. The threatening of the further cuts, the absolute uncertainty, and the instability resulting to the business interests of the country have made those business interests fearful of investing money in industrial plants, and fearful of extending the plants and giving work by producing goods in our country. If you cannot give that certainty of the home market at least to your industrial plants, you cannot keep those plants going.
Referring to the United Kingdom, at the present time we find that there is probably greater unemployment in free-trade Great Britain than there is in any other country in the world. There are worse conditions of unemployment and worse conditions of depression in free-trade Britain than in any other country of the world, so far as my reading teaches me. Not only that, but you find within the last few days in the press of Canada and the press of the world that the British ship-builders, who were the greatest ship-builders in the world, have been losing contracts for construction of ships, and these contracts have gone to the highly protected German ship-builders. The Germans, who are the most highly protected people in the world, are under-bidding the British shipyards and putting those industries out of work.

England was driven out of the market by protectionist Germany, and why? Because Germany under her protected system was producing just as cheaply and-

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: If my hon. friend believes that statement, he had better read some other statement. As a matter of fact the United States has unemployment, and I do not mean to argue that under any policy in the world we will ever get rid of unemployment entirely. But never in the history of Canada, so far as I can go back-and I can go back in memory at least to the beginning of the century-have conditions been as severe as they are at the present time, and never, I believe from my reading, have such bad conditions existed, except during the period when we were under low tariff between 1873 and 1878. While I am not arguing for a fence around the country to keep out goods, and while I go so far to say that when any manufacturer is taking an unfair advantage of the tariff, he should be penalized by having his protection wiped out, we should have a stable tariff policy which will give confidence to the industries in this country and make them produce as they used to produce. Within reason we should have a protective policy, as they have in other countries, to hold our home market for our Canadian people. If we have that, we shall have much less unemployment than we have at the present time.

speechtext: The question of immigration has always been a live question in Canada and there is no reason why it should not be. But I do not think at that time the government of Canada were under any obligation or made any commitments towards taking care of my hon. friend upon his arrival in Canada beyond advertising, as we did advertise in different countries of the world and in eastern Canada, that we had 160 acres of free land to give to any man who was ready to go on and develop the land. subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: Has the minister yet received the resolution which the Great War Veterans' Association and the boards of trade and the city councils passed the other day as to the terrible conditions of unemployment that existed in the industrial centres of population in Fort William and Port Arthur?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
I have not that. It may be
in the department. I was glad to hear the hon. member say that we would always have unemployment in this country. Particularly, we shall have unemployment in those cities that are tributary to the ocean, river and lake ports of Canada. Hon. gentlemen must remember that there are thousands, yes hundreds of thousands of people who find employment during the season of navigation, for instance sailors sailing on the boats. Among them are those who sail on vessels in the United States ooastal service, but whose homes are in Canada. When navigation ceases in the fall they go back to their homes. In this way, you can always get up a parade of unemployed if you set out to undertake that particular job. This may sound somewhat contradictory, but I believe it is correct that the busier we are in the summer with navigation, the more traffic we have to move in the summer, the more unemployment will there be in the winter at those ocean ports, particularly those that are frozen up in the winter time, because there are hundreds of thousands of dock labourers who work at trimming the boats and so on. In that regard there always is some unemployment.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Does the hon. member
say that there are hundreds of thousands of dock labourers in Canada at ports that are frozen up in the winter?

speechtext:
Tens of thousands of dock
labourers.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: Tens of hundreds would be better.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: Has my hon. friend ever been along the docks at Montreal, Quebec, Toronto, Hamilton and Fort William?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: Let him ask his supporter behind him how many dock labourers there are around Fort William and Port Arthur moving grain and so on?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: In getting my hon. friend down from hundreds of thousands to tens of thousands, I think I did pretty good work.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: My hon. friend retreated somewhat too.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
They are not, and for that
reason, I contend there is not the unemployment or distress that has been represented throughout the country. I am not alone in that opinion. I think it was late in December or early in January I had occasion to sit in one day with a group of bankers of this country, gentlemen who are pretty well posted in the city of Montreal, and a man who is respected by everybody in this country, a prominent man, a man who never was recognized as a supporter of the Liberal party, but a man whose relatives were recognized as prominent supporters of the Conservative party, made the statement that he thought it was a crime upon our country, as he said, this overworking of the idea that there was unemployment in Canada. He said, "I am satisfied that here in the city of Montreal conditions are no worse than they have generally been from year to year." And he was most emphatic in the statement that these headlines in regard to unemployment were a calumny on the country.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS

Would the minister throw any doubt on the statistics from which I quoted, taken from the Bureau of Labour of the government of Manitoba, showing that this last year 11,304 persons were given relief at a cost of $180,790, and that this was considerably in excess of the amount spent the year before? I have the whole statement

speechtext: That gathering was called by the department early in the year to lay down conditions so that there might be no misunderstanding as to where this government stood on the question of contributing to unemployment relief in the winter. Now, there is another gentleman who comes from western Canada and who is not opposed to immigration coming to this country. He is a pretty sane man and he does not lay down the proposition that we should provide, by any system of doles or unemployment insurance, for those who are out of work. I hold in my hand a copy of an address delivered on December 6 in Ottawa by the Hon. Herbert Greenfield, Premier of Alberta. He points out that his father had wanted him to be a tradesman but that he desired to be a farmer; and, coming to Canada, he has been and is recognized as a successful farmer. He lays down the principle that there are as good opportunities to-day for the man who wants to work as there were at the time he came.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: What is the date of that report?

speechtext: It is an address delivered on December 6, 1924. Now, the government cannot accept this resolution as presented by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth). If it means anything at all it means that we are offering a premium to those who do not desire to work, and the men who are spoiled by doles in the Old Country would come here and expect the government to board them. This the government is opposed to, and speaking for the government I say that the resolution cannot be accepted.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext: In a portion of my constituency the problem of unemployment becomes acute every year; it has become a question, in the judgment of many people, of federal and national importance.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. WOOD8WORTH FOR MAINTENANCE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
What time
of year?

About December, largely
when the outdoor work in British Columbia closes down and the harvests of the prairies are reaped. At that time thousands of people come from the prairies into Vancouver and many settle down in the municipality of South Vancouver; and when the winter comes on we find, owing to the general conditions, a serious degree of unemployment.

Is it not true that a large
number of men come from Vancouver to the prairies to get work and take money back with them?

Yes, but the trouble is
that they do not take very much back; owing to difficulties of one kind and another. Through no fault either of their own or of the farmers, they have not much money left when they get through. They come into South Vancouver and it is exceedingly difficult for them to get along. There are men who come in response to such advertisements as hon. gentlemen have shown to the House; they move from one province to another, and finally end in the municipality. In British Columbia a large number of them find their way to South Vancouver. The resuLt is that that municipality, burdened now with debt, has to shoulder a responsibility which really belongs to the federal government. This government advertises in all parts of Europe for people to come to Canada, and some of us hold that it is unfair to expect the responsibility for the hardships that ensue to rest on the municipal authorities. If these people are not helped by the municipalities they suffer conditions that are indescribable.
I commend the hon. member (Mr. Woodsworth) for having brought this resolution before the House. It is an important matter from the point of view of immigration and municipal administration, and it is of importance from the provincial standpoint as well. In British Columbia a large number of people who come into the municipalities find it impossible to obtain employment and they are naturally thrown upon the charitable institutions of that section of the country. There is one feature of the resolution which I do not exactly appreciate, if I interpret it correctly, 'and that is that the government should accept full responsibility for the maintenance of the immigrant in the sense of giving him money. It seems to me that if it means giving doles to the .men, no hon. member will agree to it; I know for a fact that the worthy unemployed themselves would not agree to it, for they do not want doles but work.
Unemployed Immigrants
1 agree with what the hon. member says, but my point is that if provision is not made for their employment they should not be left without some opportunity of securing maintenance.

I am glad the hon. member makes that explanation. I think the resolution would be more commendable if he would embody in it words to the effect that work should be provided for such immigrants; because after all that is what they want. Now, the government of the day, not only in their pre-election promises but in one speech after another from the throne, have given undertakings to deal with immigration, with the tariff, with the railway problem, and so on, although in actual accomplishment-and I appeal to the judgment and the fairness of hon. members in thiis- they have not done very much in the last four years. When they deal with transportation, by restoring the Crowsnest pass agreement they unsettle and disturb the whole transportation system and create a confusion that is bad for the Dominion, and they Still leave the problem unsolved. When they deal with .the tariff, they introduce suggestions having a tendency to eliminate the protective system, and so disturb conditions that capital is frightened away, industry becomes timid, and the national welfare suffers. I see according to. the predictions of the newspapers -and it is astonishing how accurate our journalists are in forecasting the plans of the government-the budget will contain proposals for raising the tariff on a number of commodities. How such proposals will appeal to hon. members on my left I shall be interested to know to-morrow.
As to unemployment, when the government took office there was an accepted responsibility on the part of the federal authorities for unemployment because it was considered a national problem arising to some extent out of the Great War. But this government on assuming office declared in breach of their primer promise that they would not dteal with the unemployment question, and they gave as a reason that under the British North America Act it came under the jurisdiction of the provincial authorities. The provincial governments deny this responsibility, insisting that it is a national condition and arises to some extent out of war conditions, and that therefore the federal government must look after the unemployed. In the meantime our unemployed are suffering. I would ask the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) to go through any of the poorer sections of our cities and see conditions for himself. He will

then find that unemployment does exist and that many Canadians are suffering great hardship and privation. As a result of the inactivity of the federal authorities the suffering women and children of the unemployed have to be looked after by the municipal authorities and various charitable institutions. This is certainly not right when the responsibility is primarily upon the federal government, especially by reason of its immigration policy. I would suggest that before any more people are brought into this country to swell the ranks of the unemployed, the federal government should look after the destitute and suffering people already here.
It seems to me that one remedy for unemployment is the establishment of the sound principle of tariff protection I am sure hon. members to my left will dissent, but I believe my hon. friends opposite, although agreeing with me in their heart of hearts, would never have the courage to come forward and support such a proposal to relieve the present deplorable condition of affairs. I heard my hon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Forke), the leader of my friends to my left, remark this afternoon that protection is always brought into these discussions.
Hear, hear.

Some hon. gentlemen say,
"hear, hear." Well, Mr. Speaker, we introduce the protective idea into this and other discussions because we honestly believe that it is the only way of relieving the industrial and commerical stagnation which to-day afflicts the Dominion.

I wonder where you
get that idea?
Don't laugh until tomorrow.

When hon. friends to my left question the soundness of our views, and we refer them to the United States as an example of the benefits of a protective policy, they tell us that that country is entirely different from Canada. As a matter of fact there is only an imaginary line between the two countries, to a large extent they have similar geographical conditions, but while the population of the United States has grown to about
120.000.	000 in the last 125 years, that of Canada has reached the meagre figure of only
9.000.	000. Where is the explanation for this tremendous difference? It is not to be found altogether in immigration, because we know that the population of the United States has been augmented by immigration to the extent

Unemployed Immigrants
of only 30 per cent, while 70 per cent is due to natural increase.
(Bow River): Is the hon. member under the delusion that we have not been applying the protective tariff for the past fifty years?

No. The hon. member is
himself under a delusion. The fact of the matter is we have not been under a real protective tariff, we have been under a very low tariff. Taking ten-year periods from 1870 to 1920, it will be found that the average duty on dutiable goods in the United States has been from 50 to 255 per cent higher than in Canada. It will also be found that wages have been higher in the United States and the cost of living lower than in Canada.
Why was not the tariff increased then between 1911 and 1921?
It was.

In my judgment the increase was not sufficient. The economic and political conditions in the country did not inspire the government of the day with sufficient courage to go ahead and make the increase which should have been made based on experience. It is regrettable that this government, through the Acting Minister of Finance, is unable to endorse the resolution of the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg, for it is a most important resolution, and in my view it should receive the earnest consideration of the government. I do not know whether we would be entitled-

Is the hon. member in
favour of the resolution or is he against it?
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

At six o'clock the hon.
member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) had asked me the question whether or not I favoured the resolution under consideration, and I was just about to answer when the Speaker left the chair. The resolution as framed, and as one -would understand it from its wording, would indicate that the federal government should provide doles or payments of money for the unemployed. The hon. member for Centre Winnipeg explained that that was not the intention at all, that the intention was to make proper provision for the unemployed by providing them with work or by establishing conditions in the country under which they 92i
could have work. On that interpretation of the resolution, I am in favour of it and would support it. The conditions in Canada are such that we cannot long continue to handle this unemployment question the way it has been dealt with since the present government took office.

The last
government too. They were just as much to blame.

If the hon. member will
recall, the last government appropriated large sums of money in an effort to assist in remedying unemployment conditions, and also, to their great credit, devised and used every means they could to get industries started in this country, and to have ships built in this country, and to have work provided for the people of this country rather than sending that work outside. In that respect the Conservative party has been consistent for the last seventy years. They have always endeavoured so to construct their economic policy that work would be provided for the people of this country, and that markets within this country would be provided for the consumption of our products before foreigners had an opportunity of taking them from us. I do not intend to engage in a dissertation on the protectionist idea, yet I am satisfied that a practical study of the question on this North American continent, faced as we are with the United States just across the line, will cause any hon. member to come to the conclusion that that policy is sound, and that it is the only one that will solve this unemployment question.

Does the hon. member
include in that word "foreigners" Great Britain?

I did not use the word in any opprobrious sense. We had a discussion in the House the other day whether the word "etranger" meant foreigner or stranger. By the word foreigner I mean somebody outside our gates, which, from an economic point of view, means everybody outside of Canada.
I want to draw the attention of the House to the fact that of the 590,000 men who enlisted to defend this country in the time of aggression on the part of Germany and her allies and who actually saved this country, the figures show that when they came to find a home in this country and Claim their heritage and rights as Canadians, conditions were such that they were not able to earn a living here. Nearly 4,000 Canadian pensioners are now liv-
Unemployed Immigrants

ing in the United States, and over 152,000 have been dbliged to go to the United States to earn a living which they should have been able to earn at home in this country. Not only that, but we know perfectly well that, although the official figures show that some 182,000 people paid head tax, indicating their decision to make their residence in the United States, more like 350,000 people have gone to the United States during the past year-those are the figures which have been given me by responsible officials of the United States Immigration department-many people crossing to the United States have not had the money with which to pay the head tax. They have , gone in by by-ways and side-ways, and passed through forests in order to gain admittance to the country to the south.
In the interval since six o'clock, I have got from my office a book which most hon. gentlemen I think should have before them on occasions like this. Extracts from this book have been read before in this House. It is called Industry and Humanity, and is written by the Prime Minister. Now if we consider his solemn and serious reflections before assuming his position as a political leader, if we consider his opinions as a student of political economy and economic conditions, we find that he had views very much along the lines of those advanced by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg. At page 237 we find these words, I am not going to say that there is that precision and clarity which one would expect to findl in his language, but on this particular occasion one can get an idea, at any rate as to the tendency of his mind:
It is the fear of unemployment which lies at the root of most of the minor fears which labour entertain. The fear of unemployment is in reality the fear on the part of labour-
I would particularly draw the attention of hon. gentlemen opposite to these words:
-that capital will not be provided to carry on industry continuously, and under conditions which will afford adequate remuneration to effort.
That is exactly the contention of this side of the House, that so disturbed are conditions in this country through the vacillation on the part of the government in dealing with the tariff that capital is apprehensive, and as any hon. gentleman who has consulted with those engaged in business or having investments in manufacturing industry knows, the one fear that capital has is that after having made an investment in some particular industry calculating that the tariff would remain where it is, they might suddenly find the tariff changed and their capital investment gone. Capital is something which walks very easily on its own

legs from one country to another; you cannot hold it here, and the Prime Minister writing as an economist states very properly, capital will not be provided to carry on industry continuously and under conditions which will afford adequate remuneration to effort unless there is some prospect of stability.
Again, on page 346 of this book, there is another paragraph relating to unemployment. I have endeavoured to find all references in this book to unemployment. The book contains 548 pages, and all I have been able to find are two very short paragraphs, not more than ten or fifteen lines each. The other-reads as follows:
Insurance against unemployment recognizes that an isolated human being, not less than a machine, must be cared for when idle. It recognizes also that nothing is so dangerous to the standard of life, or so destructive of minimum conditions of healthy existence, as widespread or continued unemployment. Where idleness is the fault of the social order-
And I commend these words to hon. gentlemen opposite.
-where idleness is the fault of the social order, rather than of the individual concerned, it places the onus on the state to safeguard its own assets, not more in the interests of the individual than in the interests of social well being.
Hf these words mean anything they mean, very largely, what is expressed in the resolution moved by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth): I do not know, Mr. Speaker, any example of a practical kind that better exemplifies the need of action on the part of the state than the trouble now prevailing in Nova Scotia. We have already had some discussion on that matter, but I commend to hon. members again the statement of the delegation which came here to interview the government in these words:
At no previous time thas employment been so scarce and insecure, the future so unpromising and the industrial community so discouraged, as at this date. Faced with a disappearing livelihood large numbers of skilled artisans may be forced to leave Nova Scotia unless relief is forthcoming.
I commend these words particularly to the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) who in his remarks just before six o'clock said he found it difficult to detect unemployment in Canada. That delegation came to Ottawa not only to lay the complaint and the difficulties before the government but also to suggest a remedy. Now, what was the remedy suggested? An increase of duty upon slack coal, and a system of protection-for what purpose? To give employment to those who are out of work. It is all right for hon. members to discuss theories and to put forward hypothetical cases and then suggest a

Unemployed, Immigrants
solution, but in the world of affairs we must give consideration to actualities. Here is a concrete example of a bad state of unemployment, and we have men qualified to speak on the subject coming here and explaining the details to the government and also proposing a remedy-and it is the remedy of protection. I would like bon. gentlemen opposite and on my left who have been disagreeing with us this afternoon to comment on this and tell us if they can suggest some other way by which these people can find employment, without leaving the country as the ex-service men have done.
I think we must admit in a general way, Mr. Speaker, that in the state of society as organized through this industrial age we find capital sometimes in combines, sometimes in the form of companies or corporations, where a large number of small holdings-

I rise to a point
of order. I introduced this afternoon a resolution in very specific terms, as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, if at any time during the first two years after his arrival in Canada any immigrant is unable to obtain employment, the federal government should accept full responsibility for his maintenance.
That deals with just one aspect of unemployment and calls upon the federal government to take one particular line of action in that regard. It seems to me that it is hardly in order that the debate should broaden out to a discussion of the whole general question of unemployment or that there should be substituted an altogether new means of dealing with this question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does any other hon. gentleman desire to speak to the point of order?

Mr. Speaker, I can see the desire of my hon. friend (Mr. Woodsworth) to limit attention to his resolution, but I submit that it Is utterly impossible to discriminate between the unemployed who are recent arrivals and the unemployed generally. It is not possible in discussing the subject to limit one's remarks to the unemployed who happened to come in within two years. We shall be precluded from discussing the question altogether if that be the ruling.

On the point of order, I
submit that when such general words are used as "accept full responsibility for his maintenance," they have no meaning unless the responsibility is transferred into some form of remedy, and the form of remedy not being suggested in the resolution, it is within the
right of hon. members to suggest the form of remedy they think the government should adopt. I do not see how the hon. member who has raised the point of order can deny that we have the liberty and the right to suggest what remedy we think should be provided.

Mr. Speaker, I will not detain the House long with the few observations I have to make upon the point of order. The resolution is not an indirect one. It says:
That, in the opinion of (this House, if at any time during the first two years after his arrival in Canada any immigrant is unable to obtain employment, the federal government should accept full responsibility for his maintenance.
The resolution is of the nature of a modified socialism in which the state shall for the first two years accept the responsibility for finding employment for newcomers. Now, our friends in the comer, with truly apostolic fervour, desire to take this text and then go everywhere preaching the gospel of protection, but to do so would be a flagrant violation of the rules of the House. I would submit that nothing would, be easier than for people to put on the order paper some broad and vague generalization and then proceed to discuss anything and everything under the cover of such a resolution. Now, this resolution is not one of that sort. I think the rules of the-House provide that discussions of this sort must be relevant to the point under discussion and to the resolution submitted to the-House, and although I have not had the pleasure of listening to all the eloquent words of the member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) I think he is out of order and should confine himself strictly to the point at issue.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
With respect to the point of order raised, the resolution states:
That, in the opinion of this House, if at any time during the first two years after his arrival in Canada any immigrant is unable to obtain employment, the federal government should accept full responsibility for his maintenance.
I think it is open to any hon. member, within certain limitations, to show that by reason of the failure of any federal government to take certain courses of action or adopt certain policies, or remedies or by reason of some matters -being dealt with by the state in a certain way, immigrants were placed in such a position that they could not obtain employment within the two-year period, and that therefore the state was not relieved of the-responsibility of taking care of them. It seems to me that the hon. member for Vancouver-South (Mr. Ladner) is in order in setting forth
Unemployed Immigrants

certain policies the adoption of which would in his opinion prevent these immigrants from being in a state of unemployment and so becoming a charge upon the revenue.
Mr. M Alt TELL: Your Honour referred to any federal government or parliament. May I suggest to you that there is only one federal parliament.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There are several parliaments, but only one federal parliament.

Under our system as we find it to-day capital has a very useful place in the business affairs of the country, and not only that, but under the present system of companies and corporations, thousands of people with small holdings, perhaps two or three hundred dollars each, are enabled to join together in a limited liability company, with a united management and with single directing force, in order to obtain a revenue and a profit from their investment. Sometimes these directing forces join together, and we have those institutions which the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) is attacking now and again, combines, trusts and mergers. By the way, I might direct the attention of the Minister of Labour to the fact that the fruit combine, which is alleged to contribute to the difficulties of employment in British Columbia, still goes on, and that the provincial government states that they have no responsibility in the matter.
Order.

And they are leaving it to the Solicitor-General to take action against this particular combine. I believe that under a motion of this kind there are certain obligations of the state. It is a function of the state to take hold of the question of employment, to distinguish between the people who will not work and those who will work, to protect the innocent persons, the women and the children and the men who find themselves in a helpless condition on account of the intensified development of our industrial and commercial system. I suggest that at present the government are doing absolutely nothing. They do not pretend to do anything. They positively state it is the function of the provinces to solve this question of unemployment, a question which is of national importance. I notice in the Mail and Empire of March 23 a despatch dated Calgary, March 22, referring to this matter, and I was expecting to hear some words from the two members from that city (Mr. Irvine and Mr. Shaw). This despatch reads as follows:

Army of unemployed trudge for twenty-two miles.
Calgary marching party iboard freight for Edmonton.
Slush covers trail.
Men allege discrimination by the provincial government.
After twenty-two miles of the toughest trudging in the world, one hundred members of the army of one hundred and twenty-five unemployed single men who set out from Calgary on Saturday morning on a two hundred mile march to Edmonton, reached Airdrie last night and were filled with hot coffee and food by the hospitable villagers and given the basement of the Methodist church as sleeping quarters. This morning they learned that the Canadian Pacific Railway was sending a freight train through to Edmonton and when it pulled in about eleven they made a rush for choice locations, neither the crew nor the provincial police interfering. On board this freight they travelled about one hundred and twenty miles, where they were ordered to get off Canadian Pacific Railway property. The Canadian Pacific Railway police left Calgary on a passenger train at 4.45 for this purpose.
The little army had to make its Friday night bluff good on Saturday. General A. J. Boulter stalled around too long and his men missed a freight train which they had counted on taking. It was up to them to start their tramp or to back down. They hiked.
And yet the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) says he has not heard of unemployment in the country.
In conclusion I submit that this is a matter of which the government should take hold. I think it is a question which should appeal to all hon. members, and with the interpretation that has been put upon the motion by the mover of the resolution I am in favour of it and will support it.
.Mr. R. J. WOODS (Dufferin):	I had no
intention of saying anything on this question until I came into the House not very long ago. It strikes me that if we are going to build up a country we must have immigration. We cannot build up any nation or country without a population. With reference to the question of unemployment, I am convinced that no matter how you restrict immigration or cut down the population, you will always have a certain amount of unemployment. Certain individuals will work at certain occupations, and will refuse to work unless they can obtain the employment they wish to engage in. A great many of our large cities encourage the dole system too much. I have every sympathy with honest labourers who cannot get employment, particularly men in the cities who have families to keep. I have no sympathy with the strong, vigorous and energetic young men who will refuse to go into the country and take hold of honest manual toil in order to make a livelihood. If my memory serves me correctly, in the early part of the winter I saw in the public press where a certain number of unemployed, I think about five hundred, waited upon the government in Ottawa asking for employ-

Unemployed Immigrants
meat. A lumberman came down from the woods and wanted to engage a number of men, about five hundred, to go into the woods and take out timber and logs.

What part of Ontario
was that lumberman from?

I am not prepared to say, but it strikes me he was from Quebec. At any rate, when he came to this delegation and offered employment for about two hundred, he was only able to secure one man to go into the woods to perform manual labour.

It would be interesting to the House to learn how many of those unemployed would fall into the class which the hon. gentleman who introduced the resolution has in mind, that is how many had been in this country for less than two years.

It would 'be almost impossible to keep track of immigrants that come into this country so as to state how many of the unemployed came to Canada inside of two years and how many did not. I was told just to-day by an hon. member who was going down to the Immigration department to try and procure labour for some people in his locality, that his time was taken up to quite an extent in trying to get men to go to the district where he lived to work on the farms. While we have in Ontario abundance of labour for many men, yet we find there are many who will not work unless they get some particular kind of employment, or who will refuse employment unless they get a job in our great cities. A session or two ago, a number of men walked from Toronto to Ottawa seeking assistance from the government, and we were informed that as they came along the road, nearly every one of them could have procured honest work on the farms, but they refused to work and came on to Ottawa. Had I had the ruling power, they would have had the privilege of walking back to Toronto again. That is my attitude in regard to labour. Many a day I worked for fifty cents and I have worked whole years for $150 a year. I have laboured and toiled in many different walks of life; I know all about labour and the strenuous difficulties of labour. But in my early days when I laboured, I never refused work. If I could get a dollar a day, I took it. If I could not get a dollar a day and I could get fifty cents a day, I went to work. I believe in that principle yet. Men who want work ought to accept it, when they can get it, at whatever remuneration they can get from those who
are willing to engage them. I am opposed to the resolution.

Mr. Speaker, the question now
under discussion is a matter of sufficient importance in itself to warrant us in staying closely to the particular subject matter involved rather than in wandering far afield to discuss every real and imaginary ill that, in the opinion of hon. gentlemen opposite, this country is heir to. I am going to try to stick closely to the question under discussion, excepting for one moment to digress to refer to a point that was raised in this afternoon's discussion, when my colleague, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) indicated to hon. gentlemen opposite conditions of unemployment existing in the United States, that well favoured and highly protected country, at the present time. This particular article, of course it will be said by hon. gentlemen, is incorrect, biased, untrue, but for what it may be worth, may I place it on Hansard? It appears in the Toronto Star Weekly of last Saturday, March 21, and it is headed:
Business future of United States appears bright. L.F. President-
That means, Labour Federation President.
-rnakas statement despite fact twenty million Americans are workless. Bad as in Austria. British and French show better ratio of unemployment-but conditions sound.
Cambridge, Mass., March 21.
In spite of an army of unemployed which he estimates at twenty million to-day, William Green, President of the American Federation of Labour, is optimistic over the business future of the United States.
President Green, now on a speaking (tour of Massachusetts, said here that the number of unemployed in America to-day is surprising.
" While it is not generally known or realized," he said, " we have at the present time more than twenty million in our army of unemployed. In fact, we have a larger percentage than Germany, France or Great Britain at the present time, and our ratio per thousand is precisely the same as Austria."
This situation, he said, should give no cause for alarm, because of the generally good business outlook.
General conditions in industry, he said, are very good, with an inclination to seek slight increases in wages in some sections while a stand-ipat policy is in force in others.
There are no visible indications of a strike in the coal fields in September, Green said. Rather there is a very good outlook for signing a new wage and working agreement at the expiration of the present agreement, he said.

Surdy the Minister of
Labour knows that it is impossible for twenty million men to be unemployed in the United States. In the same proportion, that would mean a million and a half unemployed in Canada. It would mean that practically all the artisans in the United States were unem-

ployed. The correct figure is probably two million.
Not at all. No matter how much my hon. friend hopes there is a mistake-
I know there is.

-I am firmly convinced that the figures are not in any way exaggerated, and a little later on I hope to have an opportunity of undertaking to prove that they are right, just to present the opposite view to that which has been presented ever since the debate on the Address and other debates have been brought forward in this House.
How many are unemployed in a family?
That depends on the size of the family.
A larger family than the Minister of Railways and Canals has.
Unfortunately he has not any family.

This particular question that the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) brought before the House is not a question to joke about. I hope to do my share as a member of this House in discussing the particular question involved, with regard and concern for those who are directly interested, that is the unemployed people in Canada. Who are they? There are, and there have been for a number of years in Canada two classes of individuals unemployed, one class composed of men-and I am sorry to say there is a considerable number of them-who will not be and who have not been employed for the past several years [DOT]-men who would not accept employment, no matter how plentiful jobs were. That, I think, can be proven as substantially correct from the fact that we find organized in certain parts of the country associations of unemployed, lodges Nos. 1, 2, 3, and so forth, organizations of individuals banded together, who do not work, some of whom, I think, to be as kindly as possible, cannot work, cannot steady themselves down to accepting a job and working at that job as their employer would like to have them work.
Will the minister state where they are? I do not know of any in Nova Scotia.
These men are to be found in various parts of Canada.
Say what part of Nova Scotia they are in.
The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner), the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) and the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) all have some of these men in their constituencies.
There are none in mine.

And there are some of them within less than a mile or two of these parliament buildings as well as in other towns and cities in Canada. Some of them are very unfortunate in that the condition I have just spoken of is a handicap in certain cases resulting from the war, just as truly as the loss of an arm or of a hand would be.

Does the minister think there is anything wrong in any way about these unemployed men banding themselves together in associations and trying to secure work or to better their conditions in any degree?

I certainly think that the forming of unemployed associations in the way this is carried out in two or three points, particularly in the way it has been done in my hon. friend's constituency, is not in the best interests either of those who are-unemployed or of the country as a whole. If my hon. friend cares to do so, he may ascertain from the officials of the employment offices at Winnipeg that in the vicinity of those offices every day for the past three or four years, I think unemployed men have lined up apparently looking for a job. But many of them never find anything, summer or winter, which they feel they can accept or which they would like to undertake. I am not saying this, hon. gentlemen will understand, by way of harsh criticism; I am indeed expressing my sincere regret at the fact. But it is a fact that many of those who to-day are the noisiest about the condition of unemployment are men who are temperamentally so handicapped that they cannot accept a job and perform it as the average employer would expect them to.
Does the minister deny that there are hundreds of able-bodied unemployed men in the city of Winnipeg for whom the employment offices have no work whatever at the present time?

I was coming to that. My hon. friend is certainly quite correct in stating that there is at the present time, as there has been for the past several months, a.

*considerable number of able-bodied willing workers who have been unable to obtain employment and who certainly want to work -men who would make good employees.

Does the minister think that the class to whom he refers, namely, those that are seemingly unemployable, represent any considerable number of the men? If so. does he not think that some government, this government particularly, should be responsible for those who are unable to shoulder their own responsibility?

The particular view
which my hon. friend has in mind might be a question for proper consideration, that is to say, with the question of unemployment insurance. That question might be dealt with either by provinces or by the federal government or by whatever authority might be regarded as being most responsible, and some law might be enacted to provide unemployment insurance just as workmen's compensation against accident is provided at the present time. But that is a matter which must be considered at the proper time. Now let us come directly to the point of the resolution; the resolution relates to immigrants who have been here less than two years. During the latter part of February we received telegrams from certain points in the west, particularly from the mayor of Calgary, who indicated that there were certain-

I am sorry to tell my hon, friend that I fear a considerable proportion of those1 who will not work, or who do not feel that they are able to work, or who do not like the job offered them at the wages stated, belong to the Anglo Saxon race. As I was about to say, in the latter part of February the mayor of Calgary wired indicating that there was a considerable number of immigrants unemployed requesting relief from the city of Calgary. Mayor Webster stated that they could not consider relief to the immigrants and that there were many cases of absolute destitution and suffering. That brought about an exchange of telegrams and a conference between the departments of the government, with the result that on February 27 the Deputy Minister of Immigration wrote to the mayor of Calgary the following letter, which I think it is worth while putting on the record. The letter is addressed to George H. Webster, Esq., mayor
of Calgary, Alberta, is dated February 27, 1925, and reads:
Dear Sir,-The Honourable James Murdock, Minister of Labour brought to my attention a day or two ago his exchange of telegrams with yourself respecting the relief of a number of immigrants recently arrived in Calgary and who were reported by you as in distressed circumstances. As a result of the representations made to the Minister of Labour I asked the director of our Land .Settlement branch to let me have a report as to conditions at Calgary, as shown by the records of the branch, and I am informed that during recent months a British immigrant, following his alleged inability to obtain employment, directed a letter to the Oalgary Herald complaining of his condition. Following the publication of this letter the district superintendent of the Land Settlement branch also wrote to the Herald to the effect that we were prepared to place at farm work the immigrant who had registered the complaint, or any other immigrant who was willing and able to take this .particular class of employment. We obtained no reply to our communication but since then I may say we have placed on the .farm a number of persons who were out of work. My information is moreover to the effect that the Land Settlement branch is in a position to find situations on the farms for all immigrants who are able and willing to accept the same; and that there is no necessity for any of these people to remain in want.
If yon will let me have a detailed statement of the position in Calgary, showing the names of parties who are in distress and giving some information as to the time of their arrival in Canada, I will be only too glad to have our Land Settlement branch take up their cases with a view to having them placed at work with the least .possible delay.
The deputy minister also wrote to me about the same time stating:
You may rest assured that this department will and can secure at any time situations on the farm for out of work immigrants who are ready to engage in the same.
Now then, if that is correct there is no particular necessity at present for the adoption of this resolution. The deputy minister states that they are able to find work on farms for all of these immigrants who are now unemployed.
While vve are discussing this question, I think it is only fair to the people of Canada that I should also discuss the unemployment situation in the coal mine territory of Alberta and British Columbia. What has caused that unemployment? Only to-day I have received pitiful letters asking the assistance of the department to secure work for some miners in those coal fields who intimate that they have been out of work for many months. Let me analyze the reason why they have been idle, and I want to db so without either fault finding or criticism. The facts are that about a year ago a strike was called in district 18 of the western territory involving some 11,000 or 12,000 miners. What for? In order to maintain the same rates of pay that had been put into effect in 1919 and
V^employed Immigrants

1920 under practically war time conditions. The strike commenced on April 1 last year and continued for nearly seven months, the final outcome being that a settlement was reached on practically the exact terms that were proposed by the operators at the outset. But unfortunately during the intervening period the markets for western coal had been seriously curtailed and in many cases absolutely lost, and American coal had been banked up at points on the Canadian prairies-piles of coal that ought to have been built of Canadian coal mined by Canadian miners. Again I say, I do not want to be understood as fault finding, but it cannot be denied that a lot of unemployment in the west amongst the miners is the result of their own errors of judgment, errors which have been disastrous to them as workmen, disastrous to the coal operators and disastrous to western Canada in that the markets for Alberta and British Columbia coal have been lost and it may take many months, possibly years, to regain them.

Will the minister
say if the operators have observed their side of the agreement arrived at when the strike was settled?

So far as I know they
have. But if my friend is referring to whether the operators have been continuing to operate the mines since the settlement was made, I think it would be fair to say no. But in saying that it must be admitted that apparently one of the reasons why they were not able to operate the mines was that the markets had been to a greater or lesser extent lost during the strike period. My hon. friend may have in mind the condition in Fernie and Michel, where the miners have since made a settlement with their employers for a further substantial decrease of compensation, with the result, so the department is advised, that they are working almost steadily and some 130 coke Dvens are active, a condition which had not obtained for a considerable length of time theretofore.
But what has been the effect of that private agreement on work at Hillcrest and other mines?
I do not know that there has been a private agreement made at Hill-crest. At any rate I have no details, neither has my department.
I mean the agreement having been made at Fernie, what has been its effect on other mining camps such as Hillcrest?

I do not believe that
the agreement made at Fernie and Michel has in any way changed the situation at Hill-crest or at any other mining camp in the Crowsnest pass. I think they simply made an agreement which permitted the mines to operate and supply a certain buyer of the product.

Mr. Speaker, I should like
to ask the minister if he thinks it is fair for him to go out of his way to place the blame for the present mining situation on the miners of Alberta, without giving us any reason for his statement and leaving the employers out of consideration entirely? Is it not reasonable to suppose that they are at least partly to blame for the strike, perhaps entirely?

I did not intend, nor
do I now, to unduly place the responsibility upon the workmen for the unfortunate condition of affairs. There has been a succession of disputes out there for which the workmen were not all to blame. The workmen a year ago now only did what the employers had done a couple of years before, and there is no desire on my part to unfairly criticize the workmen. I am simply stating as best I can some of the reasons for the unemployment that we have to consider to-day. Some of those workmen, I presume, would come within the scope of the resolution of the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg should it pass, for possibly they have not been in the country two years.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I think this House could do no more unkindly act towards newly arrived immigrants and those who may follow them than to pass this resolution. In my judgment it would tend to stultify the ambition and the initiative that every newcomer to this country must have if he is going to make good and seize the opportunities that come to him. In substance 9 p.m. this resolution proposes the adoption of the principle of socialism in our dealing with immigrants for the first two years of residence in this country. I repeat, it would 'be an unkindly act and also inconsiderate towards those we desire to become citizens of the Dominion, and I hope that with the statement of the Deputy Minister of Immigration before him the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg will withdraw his resolution, that statement being that every immigrant willing and ready to work can be placed in employment. What more is asked for?

Might
I ask the hon. minister a question for my personal information, that I may get a line on

what is in his mind? Does he believe that a large percentage of the people who are idle in Canada to-day are idle because they are lazy, are not willing to work?

Too large a percentage; not by any means the majority of them. There is a considerable number, particularly in some of our larger cities, individuals who cannot get away from the pool rooms, the movies and the bright lights, who will not go out into the open spaces as some of us immigrants in days gone by had to do.

What
are you going to do with the 60,000 or 70,000 men who are required for seasonal occupations in this country? When that seasonal work is over and they are thrown on the market, are you going to say that they are thrown on the market because they are lazy? They are thrown on the market at a time when other industries throughout the country are closing down. I am speaking of the 60,000 or 70,000 men who are required to take in the harvest in the west, to cut and thresh the grain and put it in the elevators.

As my hon friend knows, many of those who gather in the western harvest come from the eastern provinces. When the harvest is over, they return to their homes in many cases, but many of them, it has been charged by certain gentlemen in Winnipeg, and I think quite properly, drift into the city of Winnipeg and become charges on the community because they cannot find work there. It is very hard for us to get any accurate figures as to the number involved in the question raised by my hon. friend.
There is a great deal more, Mr. Speaker, that might be said on this unemployment question; there will probably be a great deal more said on it this session; but the particular question involved in this resolution, it seems to me, has been met by the declaration of the Deputy Minister of Immigration,' when he says, "You may rest assured that this department will and can secure at any time situations on the farm for out-of-work immigrants who are ready to engage in the same."

speakeroldname: Mr. MURRAY MacLAREN (St. John City and Counties of St. John and Albert):
speechtext:
From the wording of the resolution I think one can conclude that it is within the knowledge of the mover (Mr. Woodsworth) that there is a substantial difficulty in immigrants securing employment at the present time. Otherwise he would not, I think, have brought the resolution before the House. If that is the case, it means that the country, or rather that
portion of the country where these men are being sent, is at the present time unable to absorb the number of immigrants who go there. The mover of the resolution, in order to meet this situation of immigrants being unemployed, or undergoing great difficulties in finding employment, proposes that the government substantially guarantee all immigrants who come to this country some form of employment or maintenance for the first two years. I cannot support a resolution of that character. There is such a thing as giving a man every fair and reasonable opportunity, within the powers of the country, of securing employment. There is such a thing as making fair statements, and avoiding undue promises to men who come to this country; but for the government to guarantee to evezy man who comes to this country that he shall receive employment I believe is contrary to the best interests of the country. Every man must take his chance. I do not mean a great chance, but he must take some chance. He must take the same chance perhaps, or nearly the same chance, as the men who are now living in the country. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I cannot do otherwise than oppose the resolution.
But there is, I think, a proposal that one might make to the House and to the Minister of Immigration in reference to this matter. I take it that where there is a difficulty in securing employment at the present time, and I am speaking only of new immigrants who are being placed in the western portion of our country in large numbers, it is because they are being sent there in larger numbers than the country can absorb. What is the immigration policy of the government at the present time? It is undoubtedly to send a very, very large proportion of immigrants to the west; so much so, that some immigration agents in Great Britain are diverting some of the men who had thought of other sections of this country to which to emigrate, and are directing them to the west. Now we are all perfectly willing that the west should receive a substantial number, as many as they want, but not more than they are able to employ. I am satisfied that the men in the west do not wish immigrants there out of employment, or in difficulties, or poverty. Now what I suggest is that the Minister of Immigration develop and broaden his policy. Let him distribute the immigrants in proper proportions all over this country. In that way, not only will he do justice to the various sections of the country, but he will solve one of the difficulties in finding employment for the immigrant. The larger the area over
Unemployed Immigrants

which they are distributed, the greater will be the power of the country to absorb them. We are not testing out the power of various portions of this country to absorb new immigrants. The immigrants are being concentrated in a certain section of the country. Now if, when they came here, they were more widely distributed over the country, if they were placed here and there where there was work, I believe that would help in solving the unemployment situation.

I wish to add a word in support of this resolution moved by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth). I am sorry he did not make it a little more comprehensive, and as well as putting the onus on the government have included also some of the companies who are engaged in bringing immigrants to this country; for instance the two railroad companies and some land companies. At the present time we have the Canadian Pacific Railway in particular, whose agents solicit immigration in Europe, and we are told that it is their frequent policy to guarantee positions to immigrants landing in this country. I have heard the allegation made that when an immigrant comes out here, if he cannot get a position, quite frequently the Canadian Pacific will fire someone who is employed in one of their subsidiary companies and give the immigrant a job. The result is that some citizen of Canada is thrown out of his job to provide work for the immigrant. That simply means that when the government refuses to help the immigrant, he must be supported at the expense of the Canadian citizen, who loses his job. I do not think that is a fair policy to follow, but as a matter of fact, it is followed by the Dominion government itself. I think anyone who will go into our civil service here will find that a very large percentage of those employed in it are brought to this country from England, and if we have unemployment the Canadians who probably should occupy those positions are not there. Moreover, if they have any property at all they are taxed to support those immigrants who are brought here.
I	think the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) took an unfair attitude when he talked about the onus of the strike out in the west being on the miners. I should have liked to hear him tell us whom the onus was on when the subway strike in Edmonton took place last winter. At that time a contract had been let by the Department of Railways in the city of Edmonton, containing,
I understand, a fair wage clause which was familiar to the minister, but the contractor
