employed men at twenty-five cents an hour. The men went on strike, and I do not think even the Minister of Labour will say it was the men's fault in that instance. So far as I have ever been able to 'learn, neither the Department of Railways nor the Department of Labour took any active part in settling the strike. Eventually when the city of Edmonton got behind the men's case and public sentiment was strongly in their favour the men won and the rate of wage was increased to forty cents an hour.

If my hon. friend will

I will show that he is perfectly correct.

I do not wish to carry on the controversy. I am still convinced that the mayor has probably put some of the articles to which I have referred in the press of Edmonton, covering the point under discussion.

Let us get it right; my
hon. friend I know, does not want to have it *wrong. The subway work at Edmonton was undertaken in the winter rather than in the spring, as an emergency work to give employment to the unemployed. The onus was not on the Minister of Labour at all but on the Minister of Railways to settle any dispute as to wages. That is a peculiarity of the Railway Act; it is a clause that has been in it for many years. The mayor, when the strike took place, communicated with the Minister of Railways, as under the statute he was the authority. The Minister of Railways submitted the case to the Minister of Labour, and the ruling of the.

Minister of Railways was on the advice of the Minister -of Labour. The men were given a certain wage which was absolutely fair and it was made retroactive. That is the whole story.

Forty cents an hour is
the wage referred to as 'being absolutely fair, is it not?
My hon. friend must have been wrong of I am right.

neither the Minister of Labour nor the Minister of Railways had anything to do with settling the strike. That is all I wanted to correct.

to do that.
I will too. I like it.

I did not catch the minister's remark.

Do I understand the hon. member to say it is Liberal propaganda?

If the hon. member was in~ the House this afternoon he would readily appreciate that I was not the one who made the accusation that it was propaganda. I am simply stating what took place earlier in the debate when propaganda was alleged-not by myself.

And is my hon. friend repeating it now? Does he realize that at all
Unemployed Immigrants

times, in the Dominion as well as elsewhere, in all large centres we have quite a number of I.W.W.'s, meaning I want work? That is not the fault of the Liberal party or any other party. Let us be fair in this debate.

I hope the hon. member is not accusing the mayor of Edmonton and the aldermen whom I have mentioned of being I. W. W. men. This afternoon during the discussion our friends to my right tried to convey the impression that this unemployment in the country-and I do not think there is any question about unemployment existing-was the effect of the policy, and particularly as it pertains to the tariff, of the present government, and the suggestion was made that conditions were very much better in the United States. I notice in to-day's Globe an article dealing with that very point, which reads:
"Coolidge Boom" has not arrived Federation of Labor Officials Report Much Unemployment in U. S.
Canadian Workers Idle
Organizers of the American Federation of Labor agree with the statement made on Saturday by William Green, president of that body, that unemployment in the United States at the present time affected millions of workers. Mr. Green was optimistic of the future and the ability of industry to absorb the army of workless.
"Conditions appear to be a trifle better in the United States than in Canada just now," said William Powles-land, vice-president of the Blacksmiths and Boilermakers' International Union, who spent a month in the railroad shops of New York State. "The States did not get the boom it expected with the election of Coolidge. For the first time in years the New York Central closed its shop in Albany for a week."
Letters to union officials here reveal that Canadian mechanics in the States have had little work since October, while trade journals are -warning men away from many cities of the United States on account of unemployment.
So that evidently unemployment is not a matter to be treated lightly. If they have it to that degree in the United States, and we know we have had it here all winter, it is evidently a matter that is not going to correct itself in the very near future. The statement was also advanced that we have got very far in debt in Canada and that our tax bills are exceedingly heavy in comparison with the United States. The American Review of Reviews for February has this to say:
In Iowa, for instance, while the farm mortgages in 1910 amounted to $26.83 per acre, in 1920 they had increased to $63.19 per acre. The governor asserts that farm lands can stand no more taxation, and he proposes a stiff gasoline tax, and perhaps levies on incomes and business profits. In Maine a million dollars a year has been lost by decreased assessments on the railways, due to lessened earnings.
Minnesota is to have a supertax on the tonnage of iron ore mined, which will yield $4,000,000. .
. 
Incidentally Arkansas has an educational problem, because last year there were 57 ^school districts with 2,060 children in which not a day of school was held.
I might give many more instances. There is no question that in the United States at the moment, conditions are no better materially than they are here. I think this government admitted an unemployment situation when they called this conference with regard to winter employment in Canada. Different ones who took part in that conference expressed the situation as it then existed, and invariably they credited a portion of that unemployment to immigration. For instance, H. T. Lockyer, general manager, B. C. Stores, Hudson's Bay Company, considers:
That a restricted immigration policy should be put into force at once by the federal government; that immigrants have been sent here under misrepresentation, and that conditions will be as bad here this winter as during past winters. He thinks that municipal, provincial and labour officials-
I presume that is the Department of Labour for the federal government-
-should publicly announce that conditions do not warrant an influx of immigrants.
Then Percy R. Bengough, secretary of the Vancouver Trades and Labour Council, considers :
That they will have as many unemployed this year as last and that the policy of spending public funds in bringing immigrants to this country when residents, for economic reasons, are leaving, is wrong.
Then the following resolution was passed by the council of the district of South Vancouver:
That whereas this council may be faced with a problem of unemployment during the winter months, and whereas we have a population of approximately 38,000 people, composed principally of artisans, and whereas it is impossible for this municipality to undertake to find employment or to provide relief for all who desire it, and whereas the Dominion government is directly responsible for the bringing in of any immigrants at a time when employment is scarce, be it resolved that we ask the Dominion government to give direot financial assistance in the providing of employment of a productive nature in the municipality of South Vancouver during the winter months; and that we ask Mayor Owen to present this resolution to the joint conference on unemployment at Ottawa.
Then the mayor and council of Vancouver further said:
Many hundreds of Scandinavians have lately arrived here, and we are glad to see them. But we admit it pains us often when young men and girls arrive without funds, no work, no friends, and not knowing the language. We try to find jobs for them, but with the city full of idle men. what chance has a newcomer? We find men among them who are educated. We find among them mechanics, chemists, musicians, almost starving. And this is what they tell us: that the government carries on propaganda in Norway, Sweden and Denmark, employing agents whose business is to induce as many as possible to migrate to Canada.

Unemployed Immigrants
I will just quote one more extract from the proceedings befoife the national conference regarding winter employment in Canada, as follows:
What is going to become of the large immigration that is coming into the west this year. They are a fine class of men that have come in, but some of them may not be able to speak the Eng!ish language. We have not the wherewithal to provide for them. Our own citizens must come first.
I wish to point out that our own citizens, as a general thing, do not come first. Suppose a Canadian citizen and an immigrant are riding side by side on a train and both presumably looking for land. The immigrant will pay a railway fare of about a cent a mile, while the Canadian citizen will pay the usual fare. There is no question about it that the immigrant coming in to-day can get a better deal from the federal Immigration department, which now has control over the Soldier Settlement Board, than any Canadian citizen can get. I think this is very Objectionable, and the Canadian citizen is bound to take exception to it. I could not help but think how pleased the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Robb) was this afternoon, when he read the telegram from the Premier of Alberta, which upheld the immigration policy which the government had entered into. I venture to say there are a certain number of individuals who actually think this immigration policy is going to solve the problems of the country. On the other hand, I think there are infinitely more people who think it is one of the most unlikely things to solve our immigration policy that any government could conceive of, and when you take the whole policy of the government under review, to bring in more immigrants, raise more wheat and subsidize ships, what will be the result? That is practically what the policy of the government is. When these immigrants are coming in I think the general stipulation is to make them promise that they will engage in farm employment for two years. You are getting very close to the old situation; when a man was convicted of some crime he was sentenced to the Siberian mines. Instead of that, to-day you will send him out to the west and tell him to engage in agriculture. That is a reflection on agriculture and such a policy can never be successful. It is somewhat of a reflection on any group of people who would be a party to supporting a policy of that kind.
In conclusion, I do not think the government is justified in bringing those people to Canada and leaving them to shift for themselves under the conditions which have been cited, and under which a man who knew the
language and knew the conditions of the country could hardly hope to make good. One of two things is going to happen to him. Somebody has to provide or the man is going to starve. Surely, in a land of plenty such as Canada, it would be a national disgrace if we allowed people to starve on our hands. The commitments of the federal government are not nearly so heavy as those of the provinces or the municipalities. If the federal government ignores its responsibility in regard to those men, I am a little afraid that it is only a matter of time until the provincial governments and the municipalities cannot take care of the situation. When that day comes, of course starvation will be the lot of those men. I regret that the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg did not make his resolution a little broader, but I am glad to extend my support to it as it stands.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to support this resolution presented by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (M.r. Woodsworth), but I also desire to make certain reservations. I do not think those reservations which I would make would be more than those which the hon. member himself stated when he placed the resolution before the House. I would not wish to support it as a panacea for all the ills that have been mentioned in connection with unemployment and the possible causes of unemployment this afternoon. I do not think his resolution is offered as a solution of the unemployment problem. I take it that it would be about as sure a remedy for our whole unemployment problem as possibly a cup of ginger tea for an acute case of appendicitis. We have an acute trouble in the way of unemployment in this country. I have my opinion as to 'the causes of that unemployment and the possible solution of the trouble; but contrary, apparently, to most of the members who have discussed the resolution this afternoon, I do not think this is the time or place to discuss the causes and solution of our problem of unemployment. I take issue, I may pause for a moment to say, with my friends to my right who have attributed that evil or ill that is upon us, to our lack of tariff protection. If I were going to take time to offer a solution for our troubles here, I would commend the action which the government themselves 'placed before us last year as being necessary, and which they made at least a gesture of supporting. That is the encouragement of the development and of those who are engaged in the development, of the natural resources of this country.

If an immigrant who comes to this country is brought here under the regulations which now exist, he is, in the majority of cases, directed to the provinces or to the parts of provinces where agricultural labour is required.

Several of the provinces

It might

a chance to contribute something to the municipality in which they live. I am not interested in propaganda either for or against the government or the Progressives in regard to the subject of unemployment, but I am interested in the city from which I come which is compelled to contribute nearly a million a year to the relief of the unemployed, and this through no fault of its own. I am also interested in humanity and in those out of work.
It is all very well for the Progressives to talk about the condition of the unemployed out in the west where these men can obtain employment while the harvest is on. But where do they go when the agricultural season is over? Why, they come down to the larger centres of population in central Canada which are used as dumping grounds and those cities are obliged to shoulder the burden of their upkeep although they are in no way responsible in the matter. I will not support any such resolution as that proposed by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woods-worth) because I do not believe it is the duty of the government to get anybody a job, although I do believe that it is the duty of governments, Dominion, provincial or municipal, to help those who are in trouble and out of work through no fault of their own. I further believe it is their duty to get together, solve the unemployment question and give Canada an adequate national policy which will make work plentiful.
I come from a large city where unemployment conditions are more acute than they are in any other part of Canada. It is a British city, an important industrial centre, and we have had serious unemployment conditions there this winter. I do not care who is to blame for this, and I do not say that the government is all to blame; nevertheless I have never known unemployment to be worse at any time in Toronto than it is to-day. The British immigrant's lot is not a happy one under our immigration laws. I have here a, copy of Hansard reporting the debates in the British House of Commons three weeks ago. It shows that of forty-six questions asked in the House on the orders of the day

some thirty-five related to unemployment, its cause and the tariff. I am sorry that the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) is not here; I would point out to him that according to a return given in the British House the agricultural labourer over there is paid twenty-nine shillings or a little over $5 per week. And this under free trade. As I said some time ago:
111 fares the land to hastening ills a prey,
Where free trade flourishes and men decay.
It is significant that while the hon. member for Brome was a few weeks ago, speaking eloquently to the students of Varsity in Hart House Toronto on what free trade would do in the way of relieving unemployment here, some 1,200 men, British immigrants and others who could not find any place to which to go, were sleeping in the police stations and the House of Industry in Toronto, depending upon public charity. Let me quote the following news item in regard to conditions in Toronto and this illustrates something that is a daily occurrence:
Many Hungry Men Fed
Reveille Mission, Queen West, Scene of Hungry Crowd Saturday
Pastor Charboneau opened the doors at Reveille Mission, 383 Queen street west, at 2.30 p.m., Saturday afternoon, to a crowd of 236 'hungry people, who were waiting for a free meal. Everybody was fed, and some who could not get in, were fed at a restaurant nearby.
The city, House of Industry and the various charitable institutions of the city and the churches and charities have had a hard time this winter relieving unemployment and families in distress, and it is the duty of the governments, federal, provincial and municipal, the churches, and the social organizations to work in unison, to consecrate their best efforts, and intelligence, to an effort to solve this social disorder in our midst. The first duty of a government is to look after the health, peace, prosperity and comfort of its citizens.
It is cold comfort for the men out of work to read the discussion of their troubles in this House. I do not say the government is to blame altogether but primarily, as I said the other day, the question of unemployment comes within the federal jurisdiction. The control of banking, of immigration, of trade and commerce, of agriculture and other activities set out in section 91 are essentially federal activities, and if there is any agency which should devote itself to the solution of unemployment it is the federal government, for undoubtedly immigration and unemployment are closely linked together. If you find a flood of immigration, you are pretty sure to find some months afterwards a certain amount of

Unemployed Immigrants
unemployment. Unemployment is not a local question, it is not a provincial question, it is absolutely a national question. Every country is more or less troubled with the difficulty of finding employment for many thousands of its working people. In Canada unemployment is to a certain extent seasonal, and for that reason I am strongly in favour of a close season for immigration. What is the use of bringing immigrants to this country in November, December, January, February and March? And yet many British immigrants are misled by the representations and greed of the transportation companies and even of our own immigration agents over in the Old Land who say that there is always plenty of work for every newcomer to the Dominion. A couple of hundred British immigrants reached Toronto as recently as the middle of January last. Do you think they went west? No, nearly all stayed right around Toronto. I had a few come in to see me, including a man- an ex-soldier-and his wife from Cheshire. They were two war workers who had been employed at a golf club in the Old Country, and they produced letters from the transportation companies and from the government agency that work was good in Toronto. They were in destitute circumstances. I am glad to say I was successful in getting them positions. This was not an isolated case; there are thousand's of them. For that reason, I repeat, I am in favour of a close season for immigration.
I think the government have very little conception of their duty in helping, to solve the unemployment problem. For instance, hon. members will observe on page 1316 of Hansard that in reply to a question of mine respecting money votes for agriculture and for unemployment I was informed that while millions of dollars had been granted in 1924 in aid of live stock, health of animals and other agricultural purposes, the expenditure on unemployment had for the same year amounted to only $5,700, While for the current year not a dollar has been given to relieve the situation. In contrast with this I am glad to say that we have in Ontario a government that is alive to the seriousness of the situation. When the Minister of Labour advised a large deputation from various municipalities and provinces that the federal government did not intend to grant any relief to ameliorate the unemployment trouble, the Premier of Ontario announced that his government would assist the Ontario municipalities to the extent of one-third of the excess cost over normaL which any municipality 93i
might have to expend in unemployment relief. In addition, the attorney general has introduced a bill in the legislature enabling a municipality to devote a certain amount of taxation up to one mill for the relief of the unemployed. So the government of Ontario is endeavouring to do its part. The large deputation which interviewed the Minister of Labour last January, and to which I have already referred, included the representatives of several municipalities, of the G.W.Y.A., of the Trades and Labour Council and of the Salvation Army. The Toronto section was headed by Alderman Miller who said:
These people have 'been coming to us, and as we have gone to the limit ourselves, we bring them to the Dominion government to see what they'll do.
In a memorial from the unemployment association, A. E. Smith described unemployment as:
. A social disease arising out of a social system. The cause of unemployment is the (possession of a private interest in the machinery of production on the part of a very small class who exercise it wholly at the impulse of their own advantage or caprice. I call for a public policy regarding unemployment so that there may be an accepted understanding beforehand of what may be expected whenever unemployment is [DOT] forced on the workers.
Alexander Shields, of the Great War Veterans' Association, speaking for the ex-service men of Toronto, said:
I estimate the unemployed at 40,000, of whom 60 per cent were ex-service men. I heard figures quoted the other day that out of over 3,000 registrations of single men in our local employment office only a little over 200 could be classed as bona fide residents of the city of Toronto and the figures from our own relief department show that out of 2,056 cases assisted there were 442 families of ex-imperial soldiers, despite the fact that we have been forced to only grant relief to applicants who have been resident in the city for one year, unless in cases of extreme destitution.
We have only been able to help one applicant in four, most refusals being for this reason, or through the necessity of conserving the funds for very extreme cases only, as relief has already been closed down in four of the most densely populated districts because the quota set aside for those areas has been distributed. It may also be noted that our records show that the average man helped has been unemployed for slightly under four months.
The condition of thousands of single men is pitiable, many are sleeping in the police stations, railway depots, and so forth, and subsisting on meals supplied by the different organizations in the city of Toronto.
In my opinion unemployment is closely related to immigration, and the subject of immigration is deserving of the consideration of the best minds and the best hearts in this country. Social workers, federal, provincial and municipal governments should all get together and work in unison in an effort to solve this problem, which is one of the greatest problems we have in this country. I am not saying it is due altogether and en-
Unemployed, Immigrants

tirely to this government or to that, or to the Department of Trade and1 Commerce, the tariff or anything else. I am not prepared to go that far, but I do say there is a great deal of unemployment in this country, and in my opinion, and I have studied this question very carefully, unemployment in this country is caused! very largely by our not developing our own natural rsources. No one knows that better than the grain growers in the west. Their grain is being taken across the line, to Buffalo, where there are now twenty-eight elevators, and their grain is being milled there, mixed with American wheat and exported overseas and the identity of Canada's fine hard wheat destroyed. All the employment that is furnished by those twenty-eight elevators in Buffalo would give work to 15,000 men at Port Colborne and other lake Ontario points, if a duty and embargo were placed up to 45 per cent on wheat and have it milled in Canada and exported through' Canadian channels entirely. We are not developing our natural recources in this country, and Canada has become the happy hunting ground of American millionaires who are seizing our forest, timber and mineral wealth.
We are exporting mica, nickel, pulpwood, power and coal. If we manufactured or utilized these articles in this country, it would provide work for tens of thousands of men. Canada supplies 85 per cent of the mica of the world, and 95 per cent to the United States. In 1924 Canada sold 112,000 tons of mica to the United States in the mill fibre state, only one degree removed from the crude. For that we received $5,546,000. When that was manufactured in the United States, it realized $70,000,000 worth of the finer products of asbestos, and another $10,000,000 worth of rough asbestos. Had we developed our own mica, $80,000,000 would have been distributed among Canadians.
Canada controls the world's supply of nickel. We need fear no competition in this particular article. We should develop nickel in our own country and help provide employment here. Canada's great nickel deposits give the United States all its supply and the world 85 per cent of its supply.
According to a bulletin issued by the United States Department of Agriculture, the United States is consuming 75 per cent more pulp-wood, and consequently is importing great quantities. Last year Canada sold 1,350,000 cords of pulpwood to the United States, receiving $13,000,000 for it, while this raw pulpwood was converted in the United States into a value of $67,000,000.

We are also sending to the United States $100,000,000 every year to the mine owners in Pennsylvania. We could use $56,000,000 of of that sum to provide work and wages in the maritime provinces, in Alberta and central Canada. So, Mr. Speaker, I contend that unemployment is due in a great measure to our not developing our own natural resources and to our lack of a national policy based on the principle of our own markets for our own products and our own work for our own workmen.
In the city of Toronto to-day we have many immigrants out of work through no fault of their own. Many of them have not been in Toronto one year and are a direct charge on the community. Here is a letter from the Rev. W. L. Baynes-Reed, Rural Dean, Toronto, a splendid returned soldier and patriot, in which he refers to these British immigrant harvesters coming down from the west a year ago and being dumped in the city of Toronto. An appeal is being made by the Anglican people of the city to take care of these British-born who are out of work. Over 9,500 meals have been provided, and over 3,500 beds.
This unemployment situation is not confined to the city of Toronto. We find practically the same conditions in Hamilton, London, Brantford, Ottawa and other cities. According to Social Service Commissioner R. W. Hopper of Ottawa, in January no fewer than 897 families in Ottawa have been given civic aid of some kind as against 685 in December. The number of children who shared in this relief was 2,646. There were 237 Protestant families given relief, 654 Roman Catholic families, and six families of other denominations.
The number of unemployed in Hamilton, Toronto and other cities has been steadily increasing. In Toronto the official records at one employment bureau show about 10,000 unemployed. Those are just civilians registered at one bureau, on Front street. The latest report from this bureau indicates that unemployment has been steadily mounting, and that includes unemployment among the immigrants. There is no evidence that the peak for this winter has been reached. There are 6,700 names on the record of the bureau, which is a considerable step up from a few weeks ago. Last year the peak was not reached till the middle of February. It is expected that this season will be somewhat-worse than last year. This report goes on to refer to the large number of men from the west who have been dumped into the city, and whom the city has to look after.

The attitude of this government is that they have nothing to do with unemployment, but under the British North America Act I contend that they have jurisdiction to deal with immigration, the trade and commerce of the country, the banking laws, the tariff and many other matters. I think the time has come when a new policy should be pursued regarding immigration. There should be a close season for immigration, and there should be some authority checking up the immigration authorities in the Old Country, and checking up the transportation companies who are so greedy to get people out here that they will bring them at almost any price. During the years 1918 to 1921 the government made a grant towards the relief of unemployment on the basis of paying part of the excess cost of certain public buildings. It worked out well and helped to relieve the situation. Unemployment relief always has been and must necessarily be a Dominion matter, in my opinion, for the reasons I have given. The municipalities are doing their part to relieve unemployment. Toronto has spent nearly a million dollars; it will be a million and a half if something is not done to help them before they get through.
This question is one of the most important that is before the people at the present time. It is one of the first principles of government
that the government should look after the health, comfort, and prosperity of its people. In the days of Lord Palmerston when a British subject got into difficulties in Africa in connection with the Ashanti expedition, the government spent several millions to relieve him, the policy of the British government was to maintain the principle expressed by the words civis Romanus sum-"I am a Roman citizen"; that is, in this case, "I am a British subject."
It is the duty of this government to do something for the liberty of the subject in regard to unemployment. It is to be noted that in the Old Country they are taking action in regard to emigration; a question was asked in the British House of Commons the other day on the subject. They are going to check up this matter and find out who is to blame for certain conditions with respect to emigration from England to Canada. Representations are being made there with a view to bringing agricultural labourers to Canada from the Old Country, where the average return for agricultural labourers is about twenty-nine shillings in wages a week. No wonder they are anxious to get away from England. These people are being told that times in Canada are good, that the conditions are favourable and that there is plenty of work, so that the responsibility is on the government, not only under section 91 of the British North America Act, but because of representations made in the agricultural counties in the Old Land by transportation and government agents with regard to conditions here. Many of the men who are coming here from the Old Land are returned soldiers. Figures available from Toronto indicate that 247 of the men out of employment there are Imperial ex-soldiers who were brought out to Canada on the understanding that work was good, but who when they came here found themselves a charge on the social and municipal institutions of the country. It is not fair to large centres of population in Canada which are bearing the peak load of the taxation of the country that this condition should exist. Forty-nine per cent of the total income tax collected throughout Canada is paid by Ontario. Twelve or thirteen millions of the total tax are paid by the city of Toronto. Toronto is an over-taxed city. The people of that city contribute over $100,000,000 to the federal exchequer and it is not their function, it is not their right, to pay for the upkeep of harvesters, for instance, who are sent back from the west, several thousand of them dumped there for the winter months.-

Toronto is a dumping ground for unemployed from all over. Many of these men are British born, many of them returned soldiers. We have a large number of social workers in Toronto. Almost every church has a social agency of its own and is endeavouring to take care of its own unemployed, but that is impossible. Thousands of people from all over Canada, from England, Ireland and Scotland and the west have been dumped in our city. I do submit that the government of Canada could be engaged in no better work than that of taking up with the governments of the provinces and with the municipalities, the churches and various social organizations, this question of unemployment. The best intelligence, the best thought, the heart and conscience of every one in Canada should be brought to bear upon the solution of this unemployment question and the immigration problem as it affects unemployment. If the government will do this they will be doing something to make Canada a happier and a better country to live in.

Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to be severe in my reference to the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth), but it seems to me to be the most insignificant resolution that was ever presented to this House. Not only is it insignificant; it is unjust to the rest of the community. It is no credit to parliament that a resolution of this character should have been debated at such length; much less is it a credit to the hon. member who proposes it.
Now then, what is the resolution? It reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, if at any time during the first two years after his arrival in Canada any immigrant is unable to obtain employment, the federal government should accept full responsibility for his maintenance.
Let us examine this proposal and see what it really means. First of all, I submit that it is a fallacy of the worst kind. If effect was given to this resolution by the Parliament of Canada and by the government it would mean that immediately thereafter any immigrant coming to Canada would be guaranteed for two years against any risk of unemployment. What would be the significance of that provision? Is it right and fair that the people who have come to this country and have shared the risks that every other citizen has shared should be discriminated against, should not have an equal chance with those who now come from other countries? What about the descendants of those who settled this country years ago? They are not covered by this resolution, though they may be two years or
| Mr. Church.]
three years without employment. What about our forefathers who settled this country three hundred yearn ago?
Does my hon. friend suggest that they are out of a job?

Just a minute; I
will answer that. The man who comes from the Old Country should come here on an equal footing with all other citizens; he should not be given a preference, as he would be given by this resolution. We have not in this country any insurance against unemployment; it does not exist for the descendants of those who came here three hundred years ago, yet the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) wants it to exist for those who have been here not for three hundred years, or one hundred years, or one year, or one month, but for one day. Is the man who comes to this country as an immigrant, to share the lot of the people of this country- is he to be protected over and above everyone else and at the expense of those who have been here for years and years? It is the most ridiculous proposal, Sir, that has ever been submitted to parliament.
Let us examine the situation as it exists in Canada. We have in the city of Montreal, in the province of Quebec, thousands of people who are without employment and who have been without employment for months and perhaps years. The same condition exists in Toronto and in all the large cities of Canada. Should the government take'it upon themselves to accept full responsibility for the maintenance of these people? Not at all. Time and again the federal government have declared that unemployment is a matter to be dealt with first of all by the province; then by the Dominion. This resolution would place the problem of unemployment upon the shoulders of the federal government in so far as it concerns immigrants who have come into this country within two years, but so far as the rest of the community is concerned the government would not be responsible. This resolution goes further, and demands that a guarantee be given. If this resolution were passed into law, anyone coming to this country as an immigrant, would have a guarantee, a pledge, a contract, or an insurance policy that if he did not find employment within two years he would be supported by the government.
An hon. member said a minute ago that this resolution would not apply perhaps if the immigrant could get employment say for one day in two years. That is not my interpretation of it at all. If during the two years any immigrant is one week without employ-

Unemployed Immigrants
ment, under this resolution he would be entitled to maintenance. In other words an immigrant is guaranteed employment for two years the moment he comes into Canada. We have had immigration into this country for a great many years and there has been immigration into the United States for many years, 'but never in this country or in the country to the south of us have we ever seen such a preposterous proposition as the resolution now before us. This resolution asks the government to pay a subsidy, pure and simple, to those who come to Canada and cannot get employment. I submit that this cannot be done. It would be unfair to the rest of the community. As I stated at the commencement of my remarks, this resolution had been discussed at too great length. I will take my own advice, resume my seat, and ask the House to reject this proposition.

The hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Denis, Joliette) has made a bold effort to prove that the resolution the House has been considering all day is the most ridiculous thing that has ever been presented to this parliament,-did he add for a century or more? I do not know whether he included all parliaments or simply this one. But there are at least two other things that I could mention that are more ridiculous than this resolution, even granting it to be ridiculous. The first thing that appears to me to foe more ridiculous is the position taken foy my hon. friend himself (Mr. Denis, Joliette) in relation to the situation with which the resolution endeavours to deal, and the other thing that is more ridiculous is the position of the government itself, directly responsible as it is for the situation with which the resolution deals, and yet that government has absolutely nothing to say with regard to the condition which it has created. It has absolutely no solution for the problem that it has placed upon the shoulders of the people of the country.

Is it not a solution for
the government to state that it is in a position to place every man who is ready and willing to go on the land?

If solutions lie in what the
government says, all the problems of Canada would have been solved long ago, but it is riot what the government is saying that I am thinking of, it is more what they are not doing that concerns me. My hon. friend knows perfectly well that he is not in a position to place everyone that may apply for work. He might say so, but that is another thing that
is more ridiculous than the resolution; so much more so that I shall not take time to answer it.
Let me turn now to the resolution itself. It may permit of a very wide discussion of the whole unemployment question, but the idea of my hon. colleague in moving it was to confine the discussion to the particular phase of the unemployment question as related directly to the government's policy on immigration. I have no quarrel with those who have widened the discussion. I am quite willing to admit that the whole question of unemployment involves government policy as well as other perhaps more fundamental conditions. But I am not going to deal with the question in a general sense. I will confine myself to dealing with that particular phase of the unemployment situation that is mentioned in the resolution.
May I say at the outset that I am not opposed to immigration, and I am quite sure that the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) is not opposed to immigration; neither have I heard anyone who has spoken on this resolution to-day express any opposition to immigration, all of them being willing to see the population of Canada grow. The position that we take is that we want to see an immigration policy that will be at least fair to the people who are here, fair to the people who come here, and that will have regard to the economic conditions pertaining in the country at the present time. Suppose that the government were in charge of a ferry boat; that ferry boat would carry only a hundred people, and there are a thousand people to go across. There is lots of room on the other side, but the ferry boat can only carry a hundred. The government insist on loading a thousand people on the boat, which would sink it. We advocate that they should take one hundred at a time until all are safely across. That is the kind of immigration policy we want. We want the government to adopt an immigration policy that will place people in Canada no faster than we can absorb them into our industrial life, whether they go to the farms or to any other part of our industrial life. That is our attitude towards immigration. We do not wish to close the doors of Canada against all immigrants, but we certainly do not wish to have immigrants brought into the country faster than they can be accommodated. Further than that, we not only advocate a carefully regulated immigration policy, but we are anxious to see this government adopt some economic policy which will provide, not only for those that are in Canada but also for as many as we can possibly bring in. The responsibility for the solution of our immigration policy rests on the should-
Unemployed Immigrants

ers of the government. They must find an economic policy that will make it worth while for people to come here, and then the whole problem of immigration will be solved.
The expressed meaning of this resolution is to bring to the attention of the government some of the results of its own policy, and to urge upon it the necessity of accepting the responsibility for that policy. It may be ridiculous, as the hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Denis) terms it, for the resolution to seek to guarantee either work or a living to all immigrants for two years, and it may be unfair, as he says, but it is equally ridiculous and equally unfair to bring thousands of people to this country when we already have more people than we can provide work for. That is unfair, not only to the people who are here workless, but equally, if not more unfair to the immigrants. Moreover, in Great Britain, the country from which the government pretends, at least, to seek the larger percentage of its immigrants, they already have a guarantee against unemployment, not for two years, but for all their life. If my hon. friend wants to have an immigration policy that is going to be attractive, he will pretty soon have to guarantee something more than election platforms because the present condition of affairs in Canada will not remain long unknown to the people of Great Britain.
Let me draw to the attention of the government a specific instance that will justify the resolution. I quote from a letter received from an immigrant in the city of Calgary, and I hope the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) will see to it that this gentleman finds work quickly, or else finds what he is seeking in this letter. I will read it:
I came here with the third McDonnell party in August, 1924, to Red Deer, when I was taken to the farm to be employed; the farmer was not there and the S.S.B. agent, Mr. Smith, left me at another farmer's and when the man that was to employ me came, he told me I would have $25 and no board per month and I did not know where I was. I had to accept this pay for harvesting. Weill, I was returned to Indian school and left for bush work but was called back owing to my wife threatening to take my children's life (a job I often think now of). After that episode our deportation was ordered and we started back to the Clyde, but the wily Rev. McDonnell met us and told us Mr. Woods, S.S.B. superintendent at Calgary, had a job for me, but when I went to him- no job, and for three weeks he left me going daily until he offered me five dollars per month and I have since put it in the Calgary Herald of the 7th instant. Well, sir, *1 am now up against it and I am not allowed relief here and I beg you to use your power-
Note the word:
-to have my temporarily suspended deportation put back into effect, before something very drastic happens, as I don't intend to see my wife and family starve, so please do your best for the sake of my children. I

may state, sir, I was employed as a boiler man the day before I left Glasgow with the corporation.
I presume he means by "corporation" the group with which he came here under the Rev. Mr. McDonnell. If hon. members will recall the wire of Mayor Webster which was given to the House by the Minister of Labour, they will note that he referred to a large number in a position similar to that described in the letter, who had come to Calgary under the immigration policy of the government, but who had not been long enough in that city to come within the limits of the provisions made by the city with regard to relief. As a result these poor people were and are suffering. Surely it is ridiculous for hon. members on the other side of the House to object to this resolution on technical grounds, when men like the man whose letter I have just read, brought here by the policy of this government, are starving and threatening to destroy their families rather than see them starve.
Will my hon. friend let us have privately the name and address of that family?

I am sorry that I forgot to read the name and address. It has just been whispered to me that I had better not make it public, but I shall be glad to pass the letter over to the Minister of Labour now. I do not, however, suppose the gentleman who wrote the letter would object to having his name published. That there is a direct connection between the government's immigration policy and the suffering of many people needs no argument. A large number of individuals as well as municipalities and cities are actually suffering to-day because of the blunders of the present government. I read to-day, before the orders of the day were called, a despatch from Lethbridge dealing with the importation of Japanese, Scotchmen and Russian-German families in connection with a new industry that is to be started in southern Alberta. I am glad to think that, we are going to have another new industry in southern Alberta, but I think the position taken by the Trades and Labour Council of Calgary, whose letter I have in my hand, is one that ought to commend itself to the present government. This is a letter from the secretary of the Trades and Labour Council at Calgary:
The above council desire to know if the statement is correct-
That is the statement which I read to the House this afternoon from the press.

Unemployed Immigrants
-and if that is so, would point out that there are at the present time thousands of able-bodied men unemployed in this province and have been for some considerable time, many of whom at the present are receiving relief from the provincial government to keep them from starvation.
We would therefore request (that is if the application has been made) that before it is conceded to that serious consideration will be given to the existing conditions here, as above stated.
The point in connection with this letter is that the company which is about to start a sugar factory in southern Alberta has, I understand, received a Dominion charter, and the Trades and Labour Council of Calgary urge upon this government to use its influence to the end that this company shall employ working men now in Alberta rather than import Russian, German, Japanese and Scotch labour. To that question this morning the government gave not an answer, but a sneer. They refused to recognize the relationship between conditions now existing in this country and the immigration policy which they have been following. It has been alleged by some hon. members who have spoken on this resolution that there is some idea of offering the resolution as a remedy for unemployment. Nothing, of course, could be further from the intention of the mover of the resolution.
The remedy for unemployment, we are aware, must be deeper than the resolution suggests. Again I will recall to the attention of hon. members the fact that this resolution intends to deal only with one small phase of the question, one that 'is pressing at the present time, and that is the question of those unemployment who have come within the last two years as a result of the present government's immigration policy and who are threatened with starvation because there is no municipality that can undertake their support, seeing that many of them have not been long enough in the community to come within the scope of the relief arrangements now existing.
The full intent of the resolution is to see whether the government is prepared to accept responsibility for its own policy. It does not necessarily imply, as the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat would seem'to indicate, that the only way that the government can discharge its responsibility for the immigrants who come in under its policy is to give doles. It does not imply that this is the only way. My colleague (Mr. Woodsworth) suggested some other means; I would suggest another, and that is that the government should deport every one of those immigrants for whom it is unable to find work. That would be accepting the responsibility for its policy, and perhaps it would cure the government,
equally as fast as having to pay money but, if it had to haul thousands of people back every year whom it had been instrumental in bringing out. That in itself might be a means of bringing the government to a knowledge of the real situation.
After listening to the remarks that have been made so far in the debate I have summarized them in my own way. The government ini dealing with the situation has no policy and is proud of the fact. The leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) has no policy and frankly confesses so, and for his honesty I commend him. Honourable members of the official opposition profess to have a policy, whether it is good or bad. Now I would say that if the mere attempt to do something is any reason why this government should be supported in its policy of subsidizing ships as was alleged by government supporters, then perhaps one might vote in favour of the policy proposed by the opposition on the ground that at any rate it is something more than the government proposes to do in connection with this situation. The fact is that the government proposes nothing and appears to be rather glad of having nothing to propose.

The government does
propose something: it proposes to put any immigrant who is ready to work on a farm where he can get work.

Would the government
do the same for the unemployed?

It has not so indicated
and my hon. friend knows that probably that might be impossible. But so far as immigrants are concerned the position of the government is that those who are ready and willing to work may get work.

I am going to deal with
the proposals of the minister. But let me say in passing that if the government now proposes to find employment on the farms for all the unemployed of Canada I personally regret that they did not come to this conclusion some years ago.

I did not make that
statement. I know the hon. member does not want to misquote me but I must decline to let him put words into my mouth. I said no such thing. It would not be bad for the hon. member to stick to the truth if he has an argument.

My hon. friend is warm
and he charges me with misquoting him. Perhaps he will state again exactly what he did say, because if he did not say what I have

stated he must have said something far less important.

I stated that the policy of the government according to a statement of the Deputy Minister of Immigration in charge of matters appertaining to the Soldier Settlement Board, which statement I read to the House, was that any immigrant who was ready and willing to work could be placed on a farm to work.

I understand then that the government has developed a new policy, which is to put on a farm any immigrant who is willing to work. Well, I presume that the immigrant can find work there all right. But I wonder whether he will get union wages? I could not dream of the Minister of Labour, a labour man for twenty-three years, advocating the placing of men on farms to work for nothing or even to work for a cent less than union wages, and certainly not to work for less than would be required to maintain their families and themselves respectably. My hon. friend is quite aware, I have no doubt, that in winter in this country he cannot place men on the farms nor can he get wages for them there. He knows perfectly well that that is not a solution, and I venture to say that a month from now it will be necessary for hon. members of this House to be again asking the Minister of Labour what he will do with some of these people. The policy that he has just announced is as ridiculous as some of the supporters of the government think this resolution to be. The minister in dealing with the resolution began in his usual style. He told us that there was unemployment some ten or twelve years ago; and I think that question was first raised by the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Johnston) when one hon. gentleman to my right was speaking, asking if there were not very many unemployed in the year 1913-14. There were many unemployed in 1913, I have no doubt. I am sure that all hon. members will agree with the Minister of Labour that there were many unemployed at that time.
The hon. gentleman cannot show one word in Hansard-and we will send and get it-indicating that the Minister of Labour referred to the year 1913. Again he misquotes.

I do not think that the
minister will gainsay my assertion that he referred to the unemployment situation at that time when the now official opposition was in power. Did he or did he not refer to that period? He may not have used the words 1913 but did he not refer to that period? If *Mr. Irvine.]
he did not I shall be relady to apologise; but I am quite sure he did. He dealt with unemployment in the, United States, pointing out that there were twenty million people there out of work, and his logic was that since there were twenty millions unemployed in the United States there was ne reason why we should consider pressing this resolution. That is the reasoning of the Minister of Labour. But while he touched on the unemployment of the past, and while he was rather enthusiastic in describing the unemployment of the United States, he had very little to say, about unemployment in Canada -very lit indeed. In dealing with that question he explained to us about great numbers of our unemployed being unwilling to work at all and who perhaps could not work if they tried. This unwillingness or inability to work he attributed largely to our returned soldiers. Then he explained about the errors of judgment on the part of the miners in Alberta, as the true reason why they were unemployed. But what of the real bona fide unemployed,-are there not any? Are all these resolutions that are coming to us, are all the stories in the public press, are all the deplorable conditions in Nova Scotia to which even Russia has responded to ameliorate-are all these pipe dreams, or is there some truth in them? The hon. Minister of Immigration (Mr. Robb) replying to the mover of the resolution (Mr. Woodsworth) is just about as vague and hopeless as the Minister of Labour. He says in effect: We have always had unemployment, and we always will have. And since we are always likely to have it, he seems to indicate that the best thing we can do is just to accept it as part of our philosophy and not pay much attention to it. Those were not the words of the hon. gentleman, but certainly they express the only logic that one can draw from his remarks.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the government has no policy for unemployment, in view also of the fact that some of its own supporters have characterized this resolution as being ridiculous, and in view further of the fact that the Minister of Immigration positively refuses to have anything to do with the resolution and states his intention to oppose it, I beg to move, seconded by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) the following amendment to the resolution:
That all the words after the word "House" be struck out and that the following be inserted: the government, having no satisfactory poflicy either for alleviating the suffering of the victims of unemployment, or for proriding a remedy for the evil, shall resign.

Unemployed Immigrants

Mr. Speaker, the question, before the House is in my opinion one of the very important questions that come annually before us and one that we cannot put aside. The problem has not only been with us in the past, but it is growing in the present and will grow to a still greater extent in the future. The resolution put forward by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth), to which an amendment has been moved by the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine), is of such importance that I cannot see how any government can afford to ignore it. The federal government has a distinct responsibility with regard to unemployment, because it controls certain policies which have a direct relation to the subject. For instance, the federal government has complete control of fiscal policy, and it has complete control-if it cared to exercise it-of financial policy. Both of these policies, handled in certain ways, have no doubt been the means of increasing our unemployment from year to year, and will tend to still further increase it. The federal government also has control of our railway policy, and in that respect it has had a great deal more to do with the present unemployment than a good many members may appreciate. Some ten to fifteen years ago this country went wild over railway building-charters were granted very liberally, in fact too liberally, by this House, and promises were made all over the country that railways would be constructed1, and these promises were particularly numerous for western Canada. Thousands of immigrants settled along the proposed railway routes, and to-day they are becoming discouraged because they still lack the long promised transportation facilities. In many cases these disappointed settlers will not continue farming; they will drift into the cities and help to fill the ranks of the unemployed either directly or indirectly. Only this morning I received a petition signed by several hundred people asking for certain transportation facilities in their district that I know cannot possibly be given them for at least three or four years. They have been promised those facilities for the last fifteen years, and at last they are tired of waiting and are saying that if something is not done large numbers of them will have to go elsewhere.
An hon. member to my right, I think the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken), mentioned that some people seemed to think that, unemployment is come to stay, but he hoped and believed they were not correct. I
cannot agree with the hon. member. I claim that not only has unemployment come to stajq but that it will get worse in the future.
It is a perfectly natural law that this should be so under our present system. Today, science aided by invention is continually producing machinery to take the burden off the shoulders of men and transferring it to machines. We might say that on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays we invent new machines to do without labour, and on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays we 10 p.m. labour to find some means of doing away with the consequent unemployment that follows from these inventions. The federal government have control of the patent office. I do not say that they should not grant patents. I think inventors should be encouraged. I think we should look forward to the time when man will have less work to do and machines will have more. But if this transfer of work is going to increase the army of unemployed, we must find some means whereby they may gain a livelihood.
When all is said and done, unemployment is simply the reflex of the need of purchasing power. Whenever we have a great need for purchasing power we find the ranks of the unemployed increased. This is one of the problems that the government does not appear to have attempted to solve. The problem of financial reform has been brought forward in this House from time to time during the last few years. It has been something quite new, and has met with the usual fate of new suggestions. In the first year it was brought up, I think it was in 1922, members took no notice of the suggestion at all. In 1923 it was ridiculed. In 1924 the subject and the hon. members who proposed it had nothing but abuse thrown at them. But in future years I have not the slightest doubt the time will come when the government of the day will realize that this problem has got to be faced, and that the control of finance, with the control of other important matters must receive more attention from the government of the day. It is because the federal government have control of such important matters as the fiscal and financial policies of this country; control of the patent office, through which new machines are being continually permitted to be brought into action, and which are taking the place of man's labour; and because they also have control very largely if not entirely, of the matter of immigration, that I think the resolution before the House to-day is very much in order. I would have supported the resolution if an amendment had not been moved,
