and I shall have pleasure also in supporting the amendment.

The hon. member for Fort. William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) addressed some remarks to the House relative to the charges that had been made against the right hon. leader of the opposition, charges of being a pessimist, a blue-ruinist, and all that sort of thing, simply because he had described unemployment conditions in Canada. I thought the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River was hardly justified in giving his leader credit for all the abuse that has been heaped upon him in that regard. If my memory serves me right, about three years ago members in this corner of the House pointed out the very things that are now agitating the mind of the opposition, and described the conditions as they existed then, and continue to exist to-day. We were called blue-ruinists too; we were called detainers of Canada ; we were called grouchers, pessimists, and all the rest of it It did not hurt very much; it does not matter, when you know you are telling the truth, what others think of you These are the conditions that exist, and that must be faced by this government. The government does not want to face them; that is quite obvious; but they must face them sooner or later. The government's position reminds me very much of the definition of an optimist. A pessimist is an hon. gentleman like my hon. friend the leader of the opposition. If he has a toothache, he complains about it; 60 do I. He makes things pretty miserable for everybody around him until he gets that toothache cured or something happens to the tooth. But my hon. friends opposite thank heaven they have a tooth to ache. Just so it aches, let it keep on aching; it makes no difference so long as they have the tooth. But they forget that a .tooth, like everything else, is subject to even worse conditions than mere aching, and if the trouble is not attended to, decay of the pulp sets in, and the tooth has to go. I would suggest that they take steps to change these conditions before the tooth goes. It is aching pretty badly. Some men are actually asking for deportation to-day.
I would like to quote a letter over the name of the Danish consul at Vancouver, Mr. W. W. Ward. This letter is a very striking one, coming from a person occupying the position this man does. He writes the mayor of Vancouver as follows:
I have to submit to you the fact that owing to representation being made by the Dominion government, the Canadian National Railways, and the Canadian 
Pacific Railway, in Denmark, that a number of Danes are emigrating to Canada, and very many of them are coming to Vancouver, having been led to believe, so they tell me, that they can secure entrance to the United States through this port, and on arrival here find it impossible to do so. There being a very great lack of employment, and these men as a rule being without funds, come to this consulate for assistance, and despite the fact that they are willing to work if employment can be found for them, they cannot secure it, and I fear that during the winter many of these emigrated citizens will call at this consulate for assistance, and you can readily understand that the Danish government cannot undertake to take care of its emigrated citizens, and must maintain that it is the duty of every civilized community and country to provide food and lodging for all persons within their sphere. It is therefore my intention, in each case of Danes who are out of funds, to refer them for food and lodging to the municipal authorities, and I will furnish these citizens with a letter to you asking you to provide food and shelter for the party in question, and I feel sure that you will recognize that it is the duty of the city to provide board and lodging for ail unemployed, and if you do not desire to do so for foreign subjects, to repatriate same.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Your obedient servant,
W. W. Ward, Royal Danish Consul.
This letter was read at the unemployment conference by the mayor of the city of Vancouver, who said quite frankly that that city had its own problem in looking after its own Canadian citizens, without being compelled by this government to look after the unemployed immigrants brought in as a result of the government's immigration policy. This was submitted by the mayor as one of a long list of items of evidence which he brought to support his side of the subject. I will quote further from him. He says:
I have here a statement from the Joint Sewage Board of the city of Vancouver, which shows that we have held back work to the extent of almost $400,000 for the winter months. But that is only a small amount. That will practically take care of only our own citizens, who are the deserving people, who have helped to build our city, and who must be considered first.
They were prepared apparently to look after their own Canadian citizens, but they certainly looked to this government, and in my opinion they were justified, to give them some relief in the matter of looking after the unemployed immigrants who were brought in here. Further on he says:
So if the government is not in a position to assist materially in taking care of the unemployed this winter where work can be carried on, I can assure you that as far as the western provinces are concerned the municipalities are not in such a position. What is going to become of the large immigration that is coming into the west this year? They are a fine class of men that have come in, but some of them may not be able to speak the English language. We have not the wherewithal to provide for them. Our own citizens must come first.

Unemployed, Immigrants
Again:
So far as the Pacific coast and the province of British Columbia are concerned, being perhaps the only representative from there, and being instructed by practically all the municipal councils around there, I want to assure you that we are not in a position to take care of any unemployment outside of our regular citizens, and if those strangers within our gates are to be looked after this winter it devolves upon the powers that be, Who brought them to our country, to feed them when they are hungry.
The mayor of Toronto, Mr. Hiltz, says:
I think that if there is any responsibility in connection with unemployment, we ought to consider also where the responsibility lies. If it is true that the federal government have been bringing immigrants out here and there is nothing for them to do when they get here, then it seems to me they have aggravated the situation, and the responsibilty is theirs to that extent.
If it is true-
And I would commend this to the attention of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham), who raised this point:
If it is true that the provincial government have done likewise, they are to blame. Men have been brought out presumably for the purpose of going on the farms. As someone has stated, they have said they wanted to go on the farm, but have said it simply for the purpose of getting here, and after they got here they went where they liked. If in that respect the provincial government have aggravated the situation, the responsibility is theirs.
And, by the way of digression, if it is true that the Canadian Pacific Railway have notices up at Wembley that there is plenty of work here in Canada for men, and if in Montreal they have notices up that they have no work for men, then it seems to me there is a share of responsibility on the Canadian Pacific railway. Whether it is their thought to get a 'lot of men out and because of the unemployment situation to get cheap labour, or not, I do not know. They know perhaps better than I.
And so on, Mr. Speaker, through this entire book, which is the report of the national conference regarding winter employment in Canada. We find mayors from cities east, cities west, cities central, bringing down the same story to this government, that so far as their own citizens were concerned they were prepared to consider looking after them, but so far as unemployment as the result of immigration policy was concerned they demanded that this government recognize this responsibility-and that is all that this resolution of the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) asks. We find that Mr. Blatchford, mayor of Edmonton says:
We have depending on us unemployed and sick trappers, traders, prospectors; pioneer settlers who went into the Peace river country and have been slowly going "broke" on account of poor transportation. We have all those to deal with. Our hospital facilities are the largest on the American continent. In taking care of the sick people in that particular part of the country our civic hospital, which is operated by the city, is costing the citizens of Edmonton $500 a day, not to mention what we donate to other hospitals. We
have donated to charities in the neighbourhood of $300,000 a year, and this year we have doled out to welfare boards $42,000.
That city was looking after its own people. He says further:
As far as the city of Edmonton is concerned, we are quite willing to try to take care of our own-the married men first and the single men next-but we cannot take care of outsiders. We have a little work in view. If it is passed by the Canadian National Railway Board to-morrow, we shall have a half-million dollar subway to be built this winter. That will assist us greatly and will probably relieve the situation to such an extent that we can meet it; but at the present time, without some work in sight, we cannot do more than we are doing, and if we are going to be obliged to shoulder all the responsibility of looking after the Immigration Department's people, that are there now without work and without money, and also the harvesters who remain the year round, we shall be placed in a very embarrassing position and we absolutely cannot face it.
Again, Controller Tulley of Ottawa says:
We have a number of workers in the country to-day. We have not enough jobs for them. Yet there is a policy being carried on, I am led to believe, whereby more workers are being thrust upon the market, as it were-(X do not like to put it on the basis of the "market", but we will use that language as it is used) -and we have to provide more jobs; which we cannot do.
And so on, Mr. Speaker-oceans of that kind of testimony, not from one political party or the other but from mayors of cities, representing all political creeds; they have come here to this government and put up this story. Let me give just one illustration, one little individual case that I came across this winter in Calgary. A gentleman named Edward Evans writes as follows:
May I ask the pertinent question as to what is being done to provide work for the men now unemployed in the city of Calgary and in the province of Alberta?
I am a stranger in Calgary, having arrived here just a few days ago. I am also a stranger to Canada. I arrived in Montreal from Australia on July 1 of this year.
Now I am in your city seeking employment. I am prepared to take anything, anywhere, at a fair remuneration. The first thing, however, which I learned since arriving in Calgary is that right here in your city are hundreds of men situated as I am whose sole occupation is the seemingly hopeless one of attempting to find employment.
Is this quest to no purpose? Are the energies of these men to be spent in seeking what is not present? I ask the question for I don't know, I am a stranger within Canada's gates.
To me it all appears to be cruel, inhuman. In song and story, in alluring advertisements and in colourful newspaper and magazine articles I have heard and read of Canada, as the arcadia of the industrious, and of western Canada as the " Land of Opportunity " wherein no man need want. Is it all fable, is it all false, an intrigue and trick to lure the ambitious so that the competing force of their fellow men may grind them down in order that the wealth of a few be multiplied and the dollar-pile glorified above all things? Or am I mistaken? Perhaps I have entered Calgary at a particularly unfortunate
Unemployed Immigrants

time; but I hardly think so, for if this were true there would be signs of public alarm. The quietude of press and public leads me to think that an unemployed army is a permanent condition in western Canada. That because it is normal there is no consternation, no thought, or little productive thought, as to how willing workers are to be provided with the means of decent, lawful livelihood.
You have only to walk the streets of the city to see hundreds of men aimlessly lounging about. These men want work, but there is none for them, yet daily this hunger-stricken class is enlarged and daily emigrants arrive in western Canada to swell the workless army.
Can you, Mr. Editor, explain matters, or can any of your readers offer a remedy? The welfare and lawful existence of hundreds depend upon it as well as
Yours faithfully,
Edward Evans.
A little time ago I picked up a report of the Publicity 'Commissioner of Alberta in which I found the following:
The sale has been announced of the 13,320 acre farm of George Lane at Namaka, Alberta, to a colonization company for an unnamed sum. The value of the farm is stated to be about $650,000. The sale is also announced of the Rosedale ranch in the Bittern lake district near Camrose, to colonization interests who it is stated, plan to divide the ranch into small farms for settlement purposes.
What does that tell us? It tells U9 that the old policy of exploitation of the settler who wants to go on the land is to continue. These colonization companies are not doing these things for their health, they are going to hold up the settler who comes in and wants to take up land, and this government is doing nothing to stop it-nothing at all.
Not long ago in Montreal a glass company applied for some men. What happened? I quote the following Canadian Press despatch describing this incident:
A near riot occurred this morning when several hundred men tried to get into the plant of the Dominion Glass Company, when it was announced help was wanted. The plant had been closed down for several weeks.
Early in the morning a crowd gathered in front of the plant. When the gate was finally opened the waiters found to their chagrin that former employees were given preference, while others were kept back by the watchmen on duty.
Those in the rear of the crowd becoming impatient as they saw men passing through the desired goal, commenced pushing and the men closed in more closely about the entrance to the property. The high fence around the property threatened to give way beneath their pressure.
It was at this critical moment that, after several warnings, fire hose kept in the plant was brought out and played upon the unfortunate and hungry mob.
It is this kind of incident, Mr. Speaker, that appeals to my sense of justice and my sense of the need of the making of some attempt to remedy this condition. The Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) rises in his place to-day and tries to dispose of this whole con-

dition of unemployment as simply a matter of Conservative propaganda and non-existent, but a few hours later the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) rises behind him and brands this very problem as the most important one that faces Canada to-day. Now, what is one to do with a government like that? What can be done with them? It is almost hopeless. We find in a Lethbridge paper, by the way, a paper which was quoted to-day, I think it was, by an horn, member and referred to by someone on the other side as a very good paper, the following:
The only work in these parts is to be found at the Lethbridge jail, remarked Magistrate Sanders in the police court Saturday, when Thomas McDougall, Alex Duncan, W. B. Lissett and Fred Vien were before him on charges of vagrancy. They explained that they had come into Calgary from Saskatchewan, looking for work. The magistrate told them that touring around from one place to another would hardly bring results, but he gave them a chance to get out of town.
That is the consolation the men got from the magistrate. They wanted work, that was clear. I have had men come to me on my farm; I have had men come to me at my apartment in Ottawa, pleading for work, evidently anxious for it-clean, upstanding, bright looking men, some Canadians, some immigrants, but no work for them. Yet hon. members to my left there-one in particular- talk about plenty of employment for everybody. I tell the hon. member who says it that some day he may join the ranks of those who are hunting for employment and he will not find it just as easy and pleasant a task as he appears to think it is and not so simple to secure a job.
I received the other day from one of the [DOT] locals of the United Farmers of Alberta in my constituency a resolution which I desire to place on record. It indicates the attitude of the organized farmer towards this problem. It reads:
At a meeting of the Huxley U.F.A. a resolution was passed which I was instructed to forward to you with a hope that you may do your utmost in the matter.
Whereas there is a great amount of suffering in our province due to unemployment and whereas, among the sufferers there are many returned veterans, Be it resolved that:
We the Huxley branch of the U.F.A. ask our secretary to send this resolution to our federal member, asking him to use every effort in his power to help alleviate this suffering, especially among our returned soldiers.
There again you have another angle of the situation. The returned men from overseas who went over there to fight for their king and country, with that high idealism which inspired most of the young men at the outbreak of the war, now come back to find

Unemployed Immigrants
that the country they fought for has not a job supplying a decent standard of living to offer them, and further we find that more than a hundred thousand returned Canadian Expeditionary Force men are now in the States. I think that is the statement of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner). I noticed that one hon. gentleman said there was never unemployment in an agricultural district. Why, of course not. Why should there be? Just as soon as there is not a jab on the farm, or the farm is dried out, the farmer has to go somewhere; he goes into the mines or to the United States or somewhere else. He cannot stay here and starve to death. He is not foolish enough to do that. A good deal of the work on the farm is work without pay. I remember an instance brought to my attention this last winter. A man came to me and said, "I went into Calgary and applied for a job, and a farmer came along and said "Come out to my place and work for ten dollars a month." The man said, "What do you expect me to do for that money?" "Oh," he said, "just a little hauling and c'horing around. It will not be hard." The man went out to the farm and found he was expected to milk ten cows and feed them night and morning, in addition to doing other chores. That was a deliberate attempt oe the part of the farmer to exploit the unemployment situation and I am ashamed of that man. I would be ashamed of the manufacturer who would do the same thing in his factory. The Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) quoted with some unction a report of a speech made by Hon. Herbert Greenfield in Ottawa. I do not think the Acting Minister of Finance has seen the Greenfield resolution on immigration in the provincial house recently. I will just read one passage of it as follows:
That while the responsibility for framing and carrying into effect immigration policies rests primarily with the Dominion government, the result of such policies seriously affects the welfare of the province in creating demand for extensions of provincial services, and making possible problems of unemployment.
So even Mr. Greenfield, the man accepted with such approval by the Acting Minister of Finance one moment, is quoted the next moment as having pointed out to the government their own responsibility in the matter. I think it is wiser for the government to divert the stream they have started flowing towards the shore, it is much wiser to divert it for a time than to float out our own people, and that is what is happening. These new immigrants cannot go over the line on account of the quota laws. They have got in here and
the labour market is overstocked. There are many Canadians in this country who are anxious to get work at a decent standard of living, but they have to go somewhere else, and they go to the United States. The distant pasture looks green. In the Saturday edition of the Ottawa Citizen, page five, we find an interesting comparison, if hon. gentlemen would care to look at it. The first column is devoted to the story of the huge supply of food that was secured from the children of Ottawa to take care of the unemployed situation in Nova Scotia. It is headed:
Huge supply of food brought on first pound day.
Children expected to bring offerings directly to headquarters to-day. Twenty cases shipped.
Only three columns over we find another article:
Large party of immigrants on the way to Canada.
In the one case the children gathering food voluntarily to help the unemployed conditions in this country, and in another column of the paper a part of the immigration policy of this administration-
Does the hon. gentleman not realize that when people come into this country they create a demand for goods, as well as being able to produce goods in the country?

The imagination of my hon. friend for Brome (Mr. Mc-Master) is delightful. The men who come to this country only create a demand for goods when they have the funds with which to buy them, the purchasing power. Most of the people are brought in on an assisted passage scheme. That will be seen from this item in the citizen:
Thirty families leave Liverpool under overseas settlement plan to work farms in Dominion.
And their passage is paid in advance. Now what is the use? How can these people implement the industrial activities of Canada. They have not the means to keep themselves. They require to have advances made to them. The government is as usual so far as policy is concerned vacant, empty. It is just not there, that is all. I have much pleasure is supporting the amendment of the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine). I approve of the whole tone of the resolution, and it is quite evident from the speeches that we have from the government side that they have no constructive policy. They simply say, "We will promise we will put on a farm every man who wants to go there." What utter rubbish that is to those of us who know conditions out in the west. You cannot do that. You
Unemployed Immigrants

could put men out there to work for nothing, but is that going to elevate the standard of men or improve conditions of the country? No. It is going to place in that district a lot of pauper labour which would be useless, and it would create conditions that are very undesirable. I have much pleasure in voting for the amendment to the motion.
